nodes.response: While the chickpeas are a healthy choice, falafel is usually deep-fried, so less healthy. Alternative cooking methods could be used which use less oil, such as grilling, baking, or air-frying.

nodes.misconception: Designs need to be decided upon and followed.
nodes.response: Final designs can be adapted and changed, even during the making process. This is because it is always good to be reflective throughout the making process.

nodes.misconception: Children often use an apostrophe s, when they hear an 's' at the end of the word.
nodes.response: Remind children of the rules for using apostrophes.  Only use an apostrophe if you can name and recognise the rule - for omission or possession.

nodes.misconception: Children may not be able to spell the root word of plural nouns in focus.
nodes.response: For children who need more support, provide the root word (singluar noun) as a starting point for Practise Task B, so they can focus on securing the rules around plurals.

nodes.misconception: A speaker does not need to follow a set structure when making a speech in a debate.
nodes.response: There are many benefits to following a structure when making a speech in a debate.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not be used to analysing picturebook texts in finer detail.
nodes.response: Adults could model text marking - asking questions and interrogating certain pages. Thoughts could be verbalised to model possible processes that you would encourage the pupils to use.

nodes.misconception: It is better to know everything about a character or text before reading.
nodes.response: Making predictions can help us with our comprehension of complex texts and independent thinking.

nodes.misconception: You can bake cookies of different sizes on the same tray, making a bigger one for yourself.
nodes.response: The cookies need to be the same size, for even cooking. If smaller, they will burn, if bigger, they will be undercooked.

nodes.misconception: The dried fruit in rock cakes counts towards our 5 A DAY.
nodes.response: The dried fruit does not count towards our 5 A DAY, as it is in small amounts. Rock cakes are sweet foods, containing sugar and fat. We need to eat less of these types of foods.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that everyone else's emotional state is as it appear to be.
nodes.response: People can’t support you if they don’t know you need it. When someone wears an emotional mask, it’s hard to know the real person.

nodes.misconception: Shadows contain details of the object, such as facial features of a human’s shadow. Also that a shadow can be a different shape to the object, and formed in between the light source and the object.
nodes.response: Explanation of how shadows are formed.

nodes.misconception: All sushi includes raw fish.
nodes.response: Although raw fish is a common ingredient, not all sushi includes fish. Other ingredients are used, such as vegetables, fruit, egg, and cooked fish and meat.

nodes.misconception: Spring rolls are always fried.
nodes.response: Spring rolls can be oven baked or steamed. There are many different varieties.

nodes.misconception: It’s someone else’s job to make our school fair.
nodes.response: Creating a fair and respectful school is everyone’s responsibility - fairness starts with each of us.

nodes.misconception: Inclusion means everyone is treated exactly the same.
nodes.response: True inclusion means giving everyone equal opportunities. Sometimes this means treating people differently to meet their individual needs.

nodes.misconception: The Eatwell Guide recommends a plant-rich, non-meat diet.
nodes.response: The Eatwell Guide recommends that we should have a plant-rich diet and reduce the amount of red and processed meat, if we eat too much.

nodes.misconception: All fish is the same.
nodes.response: There are lots of different types of fish in the world. They look, smell and taste different. Tuna is one type of fish.

nodes.misconception: Once people fall out, they cannot be friends.
nodes.response: Good friendships are strong enough to withstand difficult times, especially when both people want to repair the relationship and are willing to put in the effort.

nodes.misconception: You do not need to get ready to cook every time you prepare and cook food.
nodes.response: We should always get ready to cook, so that we are hygienic (clean).

nodes.misconception: When cooking it is fine not to weigh and measure accurately, approximate measurements are fine.
nodes.response: It is important to weigh and measure ingredients accuarely, so that the recipe works well.

nodes.misconception: Sushi, raw fish, is the only common food eaten in Japan.
nodes.response: Japan has huge range of foods and dishes, of which sushi is one important aspect. There is a range of cooked dishes, including yakisoba (noodles), teriyaki (grilled with a glaze), yakiniku (grilled meat), and tempura (battered fried foods).

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that interlocking requires us to connect together using our hands and arms.
nodes.response: Interlocking involves two or more things fitting together or overlapping, which could be done using a range of different body parts.

nodes.misconception: You can only get malware on a computer if you download a file.
nodes.response: Malware can infect a computer in other ways, like visiting unsafe websites, clicking bad links, or through software flaws, not just by downloading files.

nodes.misconception: Malware only affects computers, not phones or tablets.
nodes.response: Malware can infect any idevice that is connected to the internet, including smartphones, tablets and smart TVs. Mobile malware is increasingly common and can steal data, track location or lock users out of their devices — just like on computers.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that humans are not animals, but something different.
nodes.response: When mammals are discussed in the lesson, remind pupils that humans are animals and mammals because of their shared characteristics.

nodes.misconception: Experiencing negative emotions is a problem and shouldn't happen.
nodes.response: All of our emotions are really important as they give us information about what is happening to us. It is important that we pay attention to our emotions and not spend a long time feeling only one.

nodes.misconception: Change is a bad thing.
nodes.response: Some types of change can be a really positive thing that we can grow and learn from.

nodes.misconception: All adaptation strategies are expensive and complex.
nodes.response: Some adaptation strategies are cost-effective and simple, such as rainwater harvesting and crop rotation.

nodes.misconception: We should never argue or disagree with anyone because then it means that you are not friends.
nodes.response: Being able to disagree is important. You do not have to agree on everything, but having a conversation about different opinions helps us understand each other.

nodes.misconception: A conflict can only be resolved if we agree with the person we've had conflict with.
nodes.response: There are lots of different ways that a conflict can be resolved. In some cases, someone could agree with the other. In others, they could agree to disagree or agree to take some time apart from each other.

nodes.misconception: Exclusive focus on winning limits satisfaction and enjoyment.
nodes.response: Games like Kubb should be as much about the enjoyable social experience and finding ways to support each other as well as demonstrating honesty and fair play as winning the match.

nodes.misconception: You have to be happy to be mentally healthy.
nodes.response: Being mentally healthy means we feel all emotions but that we are able to return to feeling calm and content.

nodes.misconception: We always have to do something to make us feel happy if we do not feel happy.
nodes.response: Sometimes we have to give our emotions space. Knowing what makes you feel happy means you know what to do when you are ready.

nodes.misconception: Everyone feels strong emotions about the same things.
nodes.response: We can feel strong emotions about different things compared to other people.

nodes.misconception: You need to include 'pas' when using a negative subject pronoun.
nodes.response: The whole negative meaning is contained in the negative subject pronoun (rien or personne) with 'ne' before the following verb. An additional negative element is not necessary e.g. Personne ne mange sainement - nobody eats healthily.

nodes.misconception: Shapes in Tinkercad can only be created from scratch.
nodes.response: The shape library has a range of prepared objects that can be added to a workplane.

nodes.misconception: Drawing always has to be neat, precise, and done with traditional materials like pencil.
nodes.response: Artists can experiment with non-traditional materials and looser techniques like splashes, drips and sprays to develop freedom and unexpected results.

nodes.misconception: Distorting a photograph with manipulation techniques only damages it.
nodes.response: In art, photos are not just static records of the past; they are versatile tools that can be reinterpreted and manipulated to express new ideas and perspectives.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think all Muslims have to do the pilgrimage.
nodes.response: The pilgrimage is something many Muslims would like to do. However, it is only required if they are able to do it. Travelling to Mecca is too expensive for many people. Others might not be physically able to do the pilgrimage.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may confuse the term caravan.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that a group of camels is called a caravan.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think Musa Keita was meant to be mansa.
nodes.response: Musa Keita became mansa because the previous mansa did not return from his voyage and he chose Musa Keita to replace him.

nodes.misconception: It is impossible for large numbers of people to cross the Sahara Desert.
nodes.response: Although extremely dangerous, the Sahara Desert has been crossed many times by large groups of people. Large amounts of provisions are needed though, which is why it is not a common occurrance.

nodes.misconception: Every character is a foil to another because all characters are different.
nodes.response: Whilst characters, like humans, are unique, not every character serves as a foil. Strangely, character foils often have similarities in terms of who they are, and what has happened to them, but their reactions to these things are different.

nodes.misconception: Quality is only considered when the product has been completed.
nodes.response: Quality is considered at all stages of manufacture.

nodes.misconception: Fairtrade is just the label on bananas.
nodes.response: Fairtrade is a system that ensures farmers and workers receive fair prices, decent working conditions and support for sustainable community development through trade.

nodes.misconception: The only environmental decision at the manufacture and materials processing stage is the choice between renewable/non renewable sources of energy.
nodes.response: Environmental decisions include sources of energy, use of recycled materials, sustainable land management such as deforestation, pollution including water pollution and transportation. During manufacture, ethical impacts should also be considered.

nodes.misconception: Students become so busy manufacturing their design solution that they often forget to evidence their manufacture.
nodes.response: It's easy to overlook the effort behind a product from the final photo. Documenting the manufacturing process highlights the skills, techniques, safety, and quality checks students use, proving their work, not the technician's.

nodes.misconception: Manufacturing process selection is solely based on cost.
nodes.response: Factors like product complexity, material properties, production volume, and lead time also play crucial roles.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils will assume that they know how to manufacture their design without the need for a manufacturing specification.
nodes.response: Designs are rarely understood by verbal explanation, they need visual representations with specific details of materials, dimensions, finishes and suitable processes. Communication methods will vary depending on your design.

nodes.misconception: Manufacturing specifications only include dimensions and materials.
nodes.response: Manufacturing specifications also include finishes, safety requirements, assembly instructions and what tasks need completing. These details ensure that a product is made correctly, safely, and consistently.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think a value has to be added to each term in an expression.
nodes.response: When adding a term to an expression we can write it as a single addition and then collect like terms if necessary. Show with numbers first

nodes.misconception: Forgetting to align north on the compass with north on the map before navigating
nodes.response: Hold the compass next to the arrow representing magnetic north on the map and rotate your body until the arrow on the map and the arrow on the compass line up with north, then keep the map facing that way even when you change direction.

nodes.misconception: Trees are a renewable resource and can just be cut down then replanted without any negative impact.
nodes.response: It can take hundreds of years for some woodland to become established with the same benefits. It is important to protect the global forests that we currently have.

nodes.misconception: Everyone else should know my boundaries without me having to tell them.
nodes.response: It is important to let other people know what we are and are not comfortable with. We have a responsibility to state our boundaries and other people have a responsibility to respect ours.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the local area is either one particular place or has a particular size.
nodes.response: Share examples of where we go, and think about this in the context of everyday lives in urban and rural areas, using different examples.

nodes.misconception: Africa is country.
nodes.response: The continent of Africa contains 54 countries.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that maps show only real places, exactly as they are in real life.
nodes.response: Artists create expressive maps from their memory and imagination that may not look like real life.

nodes.misconception: Every mark or shape needs to be identical and placed in a perfectly regular sequence to make a pattern.
nodes.response: Remind children that patterns do not always have to be exactly the same each time, but they still follow a rule or idea.

nodes.misconception: When observing a stimulus, it is best to respond using pencil.
nodes.response: Different stimuli, call for different methods like, loose washes, impasto, detailed line work, collage, etc. Matching technique to stimuli ensures the artwork communicates its idea effectively.

nodes.misconception: Artists start a painting or drawing on a plain piece of paper
nodes.response: Often artists create surfaces and backgrounds to work on, it makes the piece have less gaps and is interesting to work over.

nodes.misconception: Any marking tool will work on any material.
nodes.response: Using the wrong tool (e.g a pencil on metal) can result in unclear or inaccurate marks. Different materials require specific marking tools, such as pencils for paper and boards and marking knives for wood.

nodes.misconception: Any marking tool will work on any material.
nodes.response: Using the wrong tool (e.g a pencil on metal) can result in unclear or inaccurate marks. Different materials require specific marking tools, such as pencils for paper and boards and marking knives for wood.

nodes.misconception: Any marking tool will work on any material.
nodes.response: Using the wrong tool (e.g a pencil on metal) can result in unclear or inaccurate marks. Different materials require specific marking tools, such as pencils for paper and boards, and marking knives for wood.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might not start counting from the origin (0,0) but from another point on the grid, leading to incorrect placement of the point.
nodes.response: Emphasise the importance of always starting from the origin when plotting or describing coordinates. Have students physically point to or touch the origin before plotting any point.

nodes.misconception: The final evaluation is based upon the designers perspective of the prototype and design process.
nodes.response: Testing and evaluations from the user and target market are essential to ensure the product meets the clients needs but is also commercially viable.

nodes.misconception: Each defender can only mark 1 attacker.
nodes.response: Netball positions are paired, however the competitive situation will determine if players swap, if they double mark and which stage of defence they need at that point.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think defence is a solo effort and only needed when marking the player with the ball.
nodes.response: Individual defensive skills are crucial, however defending as a cohesive unit leads to the attacking team being denied space and vision to move the ball.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils commit to zone defence but others get distracted into chasing the ball, therefore moving out of position.
nodes.response: It is essential that all team members follow the same defensive strategy of player-to-player or zonal marking to avoid leaving big gaps.

nodes.misconception: Students think that Marley's message is only about Christianity and not aimed at everyone.
nodes.response: Marley's Ghost's message is one of morality. When he alludes to biblical parables, he does it to draw attention to their moral lessons.

nodes.misconception: Civil partnerships and marriage equality are the same thing.
nodes.response: Civil partnerships (2004) gave many legal rights but were a separate status. Marriage equality (2013) allowed same-sex couples to marry on the same terms as opposite-sex couples. From 2019, civil partnerships were also open to opposite-sex couples.

nodes.misconception: Marriage is only about love.
nodes.response: While love and commitment are central to marriage, it also involves legal rights and responsibilities that have financial and social implications.

nodes.misconception: All the most important people in the Jesus movement were male.
nodes.response: There are many stories in the Gospels which show that Jesus gave women power and challenged how they were treated in society.

nodes.misconception: A single person cannot shape history by themselves.
nodes.response: The Great Man Theory in History - the idea that a single person is responsible for important events - is somewhat outdated, but occasionally, as is the case with Martin Luther, an argument can be made that individuals can radically shape events.

nodes.misconception: Martin Luther King Jr had always been part of the civil rights movement.
nodes.response: King entered the spotlight following the Montgomery Bus Boycott and became a successful, popular leader as he was not associated with any large organisations.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that during the time that Mary Anning lived women did not work in science.
nodes.response: Explaining to the pupils that Mary Anning was a trail blazer and, although it was difficult for her to work in the field of science, she continued to prove new theories and develop knowledge of fossils.

nodes.misconception: Macduff acts as a foil to Macbeth solely because he is noble and courageous.
nodes.response: Ask pupils if Macbeth had dealt with his grief/devastation like Macduff would there have been different outcomes?

nodes.misconception: A single thick layer of modroc will create a strong sculpture.
nodes.response: Modroc works best when thin layers are built up gradually. This allows the material to dry properly and allows the sculpture to become stronger.

nodes.misconception: All masks are used for disguise.
nodes.response: Masks can also be used for cultural ceremonies, art and storytelling.

nodes.misconception: Children may not read scales accurately, particularly when the type of scale changes from a horizontal line to a circular scale.
nodes.response: Allow plenty of opportunities to explore different types of scales. Find where the same mass would be on different scales and talk about what is the same and what is different about each scale.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to recall the order of steps required to mathematically process the available information in order to answer the question.
nodes.response: Colour-coding the steps can help pupils remember how many steps are involved. Much practice and perseverance is needed to create and maintain the memory pathway of the mathematical processing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to recall the order of steps required to mathematically process the available information in order to answer the question.
nodes.response: Colour-coding the steps can help pupils remember how many steps are involved. Much practice and perseverance is needed to create and maintain the memory pathway of the mathematical processing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to recall the order of steps required to mathematically process the available information in order to answer the question.
nodes.response: Colour-coding the steps can help pupils remember how many steps are involved. Much practice and perseverance is needed to create and maintain the memory pathway of the mathematical processing.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to recall the order of steps required to mathematically process the available information in order to answer the question.
nodes.response: Colour-coding the steps can help pupils remember how many steps are involved. Much practice and perseverance is needed to create and maintain the memory pathway of the mathematical processing.

nodes.misconception: In 3D or sculptural work, mass is just about how much it weighs and its physical presence.
nodes.response: Mass can be symbolic due to the materials used. Materials can carry more or less visual weight.

nodes.misconception: All peaks in a mass spectrum represent intact (and neutral) molecules or atoms.
nodes.response: Clarify that in mass spectrometry, all detected peaks represent ionised species, not neutral molecules or atoms. The peaks can correspond to either the molecular ion (M⁺) or smaller ionised fragments, as well as different isotopes of an element.

nodes.misconception: Annotations can replace the need for a clear and accurate sketch.
nodes.response: Annotation provides further explanation or clarification on what is not visible in the sketch.

nodes.misconception: I can effectively practise my presentation in my head.
nodes.response: Although it is good to think about your presentation, you will need to practise delivering it out loud. This will give you a much better idea of timing and pace.

nodes.misconception: There may be issues with group dynamics as pupils have to negotiate which movements they will use when working in bigger groups. Not all pupils in the group may be able to perform the movements.
nodes.response: Pupils may have to delegate a leader or be encouraged to listen to each other when working in bigger groups. Pupils may have to consider adapting their sequences when working with bigger groups.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to distinguish between a matching and mirroring movement. Pupils struggle to execute their movements simultaneously.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to work with peers to check whether a movement is matching or mirroring. Pupils should work on communication to improve their synchronisation.

nodes.misconception: Forming a capital letter is just doing the lower case letter formation bigger.
nodes.response: Highlight every time the lower case and capital letter is different so it is clear the formation is different not just the size.

nodes.misconception: All film music has to be precise to the second to fit the action perfectly.
nodes.response: Some film scenes do have to be exact where the music mirrors precisely what is happening on screen, but much film music is about creating the correct atmosphere and feel and this can be just as important when composing programmatic music.

nodes.misconception: When pupils perform their sequence on apparatus, they lose control, extension and flow.
nodes.response: Make sure that pupils carefully consider how they can adapt their sequences to work on apparatus so they don't lose quality. Pupils can also focus on communication to help improve the quality of their sequence on apparatus.

nodes.misconception: One pupil always leads the other. Only one pupil can perform the movement with quality.
nodes.response: Use strategies such as counting or music to help pupils move at the same time. Encourage pupils to ensure that both of them can perform the skills, and if they can't, they should work on improving or changing the movement.

nodes.misconception: Textiles are not made from fossil fuels.
nodes.response: Synthetic fibres are usually made from fossil fuels such a polyester and ripstop nylon.

nodes.misconception: The cheapest material is always the best choice.
nodes.response: Material selection involves balancing multiple factors, such as strength, durability, weight, sustainability, and ease of manufacturing; in addition to cost.

nodes.misconception: The atmosphere is made up of mainly oxygen and carbon dioxide.
nodes.response: Explain that Earth's atmosphere is delicately balanced. There is enough oxygen to maintain life, and enough carbon dioxide to help insulate the planet, maintaining the temperature that allows life to exist.

nodes.misconception: The water cycle only includes the processes of evaporation from the Earth's surface to the atmosphere and condensation returning water to the Earth.
nodes.response: There is exemplification of how the water cycle involves percolation of water into the ground and how plants use this water. Some of this is released by transpiration.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may think that soft means smooth. Younger pupils may find it hard to describe a material based only on its properties (and not its function).
nodes.response: Opportunities to rehearse expressing ideas and describing properties. Teacher to model and correct as necessary, making clear the difference between the function of an object and the properties of its material(s).

nodes.misconception: There is only one suitable material for each product.
nodes.response: There are many different materials which can be suitable once a choice has been made; it is important to explain and justify this.

nodes.misconception: Recycling is good for the environment.
nodes.response: Recycling ensures that materials are useful for longer before being discarded, but the processing is an envionmental cost.

nodes.misconception: The word material can be challenging, it has a different meaning in everyday life. Understanding that an alloy is a mixture and not a compound is hard because the elements are difficult to separate.
nodes.response: Provide lots of different examples of materials and use the word correctly within the scientific contexts. An alloy is the exception to the rule and is separated by thermal or chemical processes.

nodes.misconception: Paper and boards are often seen as weak materials.
nodes.response: Many types of paper and boards are designed to be robust, such as corrugated cardboard used for packaging.

nodes.misconception: Choosing materials is always based on aesthetics.
nodes.response: Many factors determine the material choice, such as the purpose and environment of the product. For example, MDF is absorbent and not suitable for damp or humid places, unless finished with a waterproof layer.

nodes.misconception: Choosing materials is always based on aesthetics.
nodes.response: Many factors determine the material choice, such as the purpose and environment of the product. For example, cotton calico is absorbent and not suitable for damp or humid places unless finished with a waterproof layer.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may instinctively classify objects by observational similarities or through knowledge of use rather than by the material from which the objects are made.
nodes.response: Examples of different objects made from different materials to promote discussion of the properties of materials.

nodes.misconception: Children may instinctively classify objects by observational similarities or through knowledge of use rather than by the material from which the objects are made.
nodes.response: Reminders of the difference between the object, what it is used for, and the material it is made from. Use of real-life objects for children to explore to aid this understanding.

nodes.misconception: Mathematical operations cannot be performed on items held in a list; the items must first be stored in a new variable.
nodes.response: Mathematical operations can be performed directly on list items by using an index value to reference the value used.

nodes.misconception: Women were forbidden from ruling in their own right in England during the medieval period.
nodes.response: The first time the concept of a woman ruling in her own right in England occurred it took everyone by surprise. No one had considered that a woman might rule alone, so there was no law preventing it from happening.

nodes.misconception: Once a king dies or is taken prisoner, that is the end of the war.
nodes.response: Although a king is very important, there are many examples throughout history of a king's followers continuing to fight on successfully after their leader has been killed or captured.

nodes.misconception: Women in England were not allowed to fight in wars.
nodes.response: We have many examples of women leading the defence of castles throughout English history, and occasionally leading the attack on enemy territory as well.  It was uncommon, but not unheard of.

nodes.misconception: It has always been illegal for children to get married.
nodes.response: Throughout history, royal children were regularly betrothed at a young age in order to secure alliances between nations. Marriage followed later when the children had grown up, although they regularly still married younger than we do today.

nodes.misconception: Barons must obey the their monarch's orders.
nodes.response: Although this is true in theory, in reality the barons and their monarch worked as a partnership: the monarch relied upon the barons and if they weren't doing a good enough job, they could expect to lose the support of their barons.

nodes.misconception: Angelou copied Dunbar. Copying is not allowed.
nodes.response: Many writers learn from, and are inspired by, others. Angelou's poem is very different to Dunbar's - her personal style and voice come through - but the central metaphor 'speaks' from one poem to another, developing a relationship between them.

nodes.misconception: You shouldn't talk about poems as a group. This will make your comments too general.
nodes.response: You can make clear comments about a poet's work as a whole, as long as these comments are supported by specific examples from specific poems.

nodes.misconception: Mesoamerican civilizations were primitive or less advanced compared to European counterparts.
nodes.response: Mesoamerican societies achieved remarkable advancements in architecture, mathematics, astronomy, agriculture, and writing systems. E.g., the Maya developed calendar systems and made contributions to mathematics, including the concept of zero.

nodes.misconception: When you skip, you always travel forwards.
nodes.response: Skipping often involves travelling forwards, but it can also be performed on the spot or even travelling backwards.

nodes.misconception: All relationships are the same, and we interact with all people in the same way.
nodes.response: We form many different relationships with other people throughout our lives. The way we interact with people will depend on the relationship we have with them.

nodes.misconception: Final consonants that are pronounced in English are also pronounced in French.
nodes.response: The letters d, s, t and x are usually silent at the end of words in French.

nodes.misconception: The means of salvation are grace, Jesus, biblical law and the Holy Spirit, which are distinct and separate from each other.
nodes.response: These concepts are intertwined. Grace can come through Jesus, the law of the Bible and the Holy Spirit.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might count a part square - such as a triangle - as one square unit.
nodes.response: The slides show two parts moving together to make a whole square. Cutting out and physically moving the parts is an effective strategy.

nodes.misconception: Some children may find it difficult to align the cubes with the ends of the objects, particularly when the object cannot be placed close to the cubes because it is curved or an irregular shape.
nodes.response: Use objects such as pencils and pens that can be placed close to the cubes, or support children with aligning the start of the object with the cubes by placing them both against a wall or a straight object such as a book.

nodes.misconception: The length or height of an object is the numerical value at the end of the ruler (if not at zero).
nodes.response: If an object is not measured from zero, its length is the difference between the numerical value at the start and end of the object.

nodes.misconception: Children may align the end of their object with the end of the ruler, rather than zero.
nodes.response: Use a sticker or coloured pen to highlight the zero on the ruler so that children's attention is drawn to the zero when they are measuring length using a ruler.

nodes.misconception: Children may not use cubes accurately, for example leaving gaps between the objects. They may also miscount the cubes.
nodes.response: Encourage children to build a straight line of cubes with no gaps first, then place the object they want to measure along the line of cubes. Encourage them to touch each cube as they count.

nodes.misconception: Children may not use objects to measure accurately, for example following the shape of the object they are measuring rather than placing objects in a straight line. They may miscount the objects.
nodes.response: Encourage children to build a straight line of objects with no gaps first, then place the object they want to measure along the line. Encourage them to touch each object as they count.

nodes.misconception: Children may not use objects to measure accurately, for example leaving gaps between the objects. They may also miscount the objects.
nodes.response: Encourage children to build a straight line of objects with no gaps first, then place the object they want to measure along the line. Encourage them to touch each object as they count.

nodes.misconception: Composition of 1,000 is Year 4 content so children may make mistakes when giving masses in kg and g.
nodes.response: Use of stem sentences to help: 1,000 is composed of __ equal parts of __.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that an area of one square metre has to be in the shape of a square.
nodes.response: Take two large pieces of paper, each one square metre, and fold them in half in different ways. Bring them together to form a square metre.

nodes.misconception: Misreading of scales by counting marks rather than equal parts in between the marked intervals.
nodes.response: Remember to look at the number of equal parts in between the marked intervals then use your knowledge of the composition of 100.

nodes.misconception: Pupils incorrectly place the protractor on the angle and therefore cannot measure the angle. Pupils use the incorrect scale to read the angle.
nodes.response: Stress the importance of using the middle spot on the protractor to line this up with the vertex of the angle as well as placing one of the lines on a zero line, ensuring the remaining line crosses the scale of the protractor.

nodes.misconception: Children further learn about the composition of 1,000 in Y4, so may make mistakes in reading scales.
nodes.response: Rehearse 1,000 is composed of two equal parts of 500 ml, four equal parts of 250 ml, five equal parts of 200 ml, 10 equal parts of 100 ml.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may compare their progress to other pupils and feel disappointed if others have made a faster rate of progress.
nodes.response: Progress is personal and depends on many things - starting fitness, goals, technique and even how well rested you are on test day. Even small amounts of progress should be celebrated.

nodes.misconception: Mega is larger than giga.
nodes.response: The order of prefixes from smallest to largest is kilo, mega, giga, tera.

nodes.misconception: Bits and bytes are the same thing. They all refer to binary numbers.
nodes.response: A bit is the smallest unit of data. A byte is a group of 8 bits and is used to summarise larger sequences of bits in a more convenient way.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may compare the accelerations of objects on the basis of final velocities and may fail to take into account the time interval over which the change in velocity occurred.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with opportunity to analyse measurements of changes in velocity in which the starting velocities vary. A pair of light gates at two positions along the ramp will allow this.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may compare the accelerations of objects on the basis of final velocities and may fail to take into account the time interval over which the change in velocity occurred.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with opportunity to analyse measurements of changes in velocity in which the starting velocities vary. A pair of light gates at two positions along the ramp will allow this.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may compare the accelerations of objects on the basis of final velocities and may fail to take into account the time interval over which the change in velocity occurred.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with opportunity to analyse measurements of changes in velocity in which the starting velocities vary. A pair of light gates at two positions along the ramp will allow this.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that final velocity is proportional to acceleration and do not take into account the time over which an object is accelerating.
nodes.response: Compare how many times greater the calculated accelerations of two sets of readings are compared to how many times greater the final velocities are.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that final velocity is proportional to acceleration and do not take into account the time over which an object is accelerating.
nodes.response: Compare how many times greater the calculated accelerations of two sets of readings are compared to how many times greater the final velocities are.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that final velocity is proportional to acceleration and do not take into account the time over which an object is accelerating.
nodes.response: Compare how many times greater the calculated accelerations of two sets of readings are compared to how many times greater the final velocities are.

nodes.misconception: GDP per capita is the most effective way to measure development.
nodes.response: Although useful, GDP per capita is not as effective as composite indicators such as HDI, which include a measure of health and education

nodes.misconception: Children may not be familiar with tally charts as a method of recording.
nodes.response: Practise reading and writing tallies prior to the lesson would support their understanding.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often analyse circuits sequentially, starting from the battery, which makes predicting what current does at a junction impossible.
nodes.response: Teach pupils to analyse each complete loop of a parallel circuit as whole loops. The currents through each loop then add to give the current through the battery (rather than current from the battery miraculously ‘knowing’ how to split at a junction).

nodes.misconception: Pupils confuse the mass or weight of an object with density.
nodes.response: Provide pupils with a range of objects of varying sizes that they are going to measure the density of. Before measuring density, ask the pupils to rank the objects in order of density with explanations. Compare results to the list after measurements.

nodes.misconception: That everyone in a country with a high GNI is well off, with a good quality of life.
nodes.response: A country’s income is not equally divided by everyone who lives there. This is why GNI per head should be used along side other measures in order to understand differences in quality of life.

nodes.misconception: Earthquakes are their strongest at their epicentre.
nodes.response: Earthquakes are felt their strongest at their epicentre as that is where humans first feel them. Earthquakes are actually their strongest at their focus point, but humans do not feel them until seismic waves have travelled through the Earth's crust.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often hold a consumption model of electric current, believing it is used up in a circuit. They misuse the terms voltage, current and electricity, and may choose a voltmeter to measure current.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to investigate the size of the current through a range of different conductors (and insulators) using an ammeter in a simple circuit. This will help them become familiar with the ammeter and its correct use.

nodes.misconception: Pupils are often unable to match their experience of different forces with forces in newtons.
nodes.response: Pupils are provided with opportunity to both measure and describe a range of forces.

nodes.misconception: It is important for the same person to take all the measurements.
nodes.response: Emphasise that if the method is a good one then everyone carrying it out carefully should get similar results that show the same pattern (the results are repeatable and reproducible).

nodes.misconception: When the trolley is released, it speeds up quickly at the start and then rolls at a constant speed.
nodes.response: Show a video of an accelerating trolley in slow motion identifying the distance travelled in successive equal intervals of time.

nodes.misconception: When the trolley is released it speeds up quickly at the start and then rolls at a constant speed.
nodes.response: Show a video of an accelerating trolley in slow motion, identifying the distance travelled in successive equal intervals of time.

nodes.misconception: The length or height of an object is the numerical value at the end of the ruler (if not at zero).
nodes.response: If an object is not measured from zero, its length is the difference between the numerical value at the start and end of the object.

nodes.misconception: Only shiny surfaces reflect light. Light does not always travel in straight lines when it bounces off a mirror.
nodes.response: The lesson gives the children a chance to explore reflection of light in mirrors to see for themselves that it does reflect in a straight line.

nodes.misconception: To measure the angle where light hits a surface, measure in between the beam of light and the surface.
nodes.response: The lesson gives children an opportunity to explore a new concept: the normal line. They should become familiar with measuring between the beam of light and the normal line drawn at a right angle to the surface.

nodes.misconception: A systematic error can be spotted by taking repeat readings.
nodes.response: Discuss why the heating of the beaker when measuring specific heat capacity of water will always increase energy measured by the same proportion.

nodes.misconception: Pupils commonly confuse instantaneous and average speeds.
nodes.response: Be very careful when using the word speed, always use 'average' or 'instantaneous' explicitly, linking average speed to a time period.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the constant force on the trolley will cause it to move at a constant speed.
nodes.response: Demonstrate that the trolly speeds up as it rolls, by finding speed near the start and near the end of the ramp.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often estimate the temperature of an object based on its materials, rather than the temperature of the surroundings.
nodes.response: Measure the temperature of several things that are all at room temperature such as water, sand and the air, in order to show that they are all the same.

nodes.misconception: The gradient of an I–V graph is equal to 1/R because I = V ÷ R.
nodes.response: Explain how the equation for a straight line graph y = mx + c does not apply in this case because the graph is not a straight line.

nodes.misconception: The terms current, voltage, resistance, energy and power, together with the properties of each, are often mixed up.
nodes.response: As each term is introduced during this lesson, spend a few moments checking pupils’ understanding.

nodes.misconception: Many pupils believe that in order to determine a population size within a habitat, all organisms within a habitat have to be counted.
nodes.response: Populations can be estimated using sampling techniques. As long as a sample size is large enough, it will provide a reliable estimate of the population size. Pupils should understand that counting all individuals in a habitat is very difficult to do.

nodes.misconception: If measurements are repeatable (or precise) then they will also be accurate.
nodes.response: Repeatable (or precise) measurements may involve a systematic error making them inaccurate.

nodes.misconception: Calculating a mean of repeat readings reduces (random) errors in measurements.
nodes.response: Calculating a mean reduces the effect that random errors have on a final result. The random errors in the original readings are unaffected.

nodes.misconception: Children may read the scale incorrectly - confusion between equal parts and marks on the scale.
nodes.response: The scale is a number line. Remember to look at the number of equal parts between the marked numbers not the marks themselves.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that volume of sound cannot be measured, as they may not have encountered equipment or the units of measurement for doing so.
nodes.response: Allow opportunities to measure the volume of a range of everyday sounds so that pupils become familiar with decibel levels.

nodes.misconception: Pupils are likely to use the words current, voltage, power, and energy interchangeably. They often have a consumption model of current and believe that voltage flows through a circuit.
nodes.response: It is essential that pupils distinguish between the current flowing through the circuit (which is conserved), the energy stored in the cell or battery and transferred elsewhere, and the voltage across the cell, battery or component.

nodes.misconception: In the equation for the speed of a wave, v = f x λ, speed is dependent on frequency and/or wavelength.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the speed of a wave depends only on the wave medium and not on frequency or wavelength.

nodes.misconception: In the equation for the speed of a wave, v = f x λ, speed is dependent on frequency and/or wavelength.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the speed of a wave depends only on the wave medium and not on frequency or wavelength.

nodes.misconception: Frequency or wavelength of waves on a string will affect the wave speed.
nodes.response: The speed of waves on a string only depends on the properties of the wave medium (the string) e.g. tension, density

nodes.misconception: Tidal volume is the amount of air breathed in and out per breath and the lungs completely empty of air when we expire.
nodes.response: Tidal volume is the volume of air breathed in or out per breadth and it increases during exercise to enable more air and hence exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide to occur. A residual volume of air always remains in the lungs to keep them inflated.

nodes.misconception: To help the split pin to turn, create a bigger hole.
nodes.response: If the hole is too big, this will allow the split pin to wobble and cause the mechanism to not work accurately. Use a standard pencil and turn the split pin when it is in place and this will help it the lever to move smoothly.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may struggle in the first learning cycle with where each object should be placed.
nodes.response: The closer to the observation point an object is, the larger it appears to be. So if we want an object to appear larger than something else, we need to place it closer to the camera.

nodes.misconception: Substituting the wrong values into the formulas.
nodes.response: The formulas are written in words so ensure pupils check that what they are substituting is the correct value by rereading the description for each value.

nodes.misconception: All medieval approaches to treatment and prevention were ineffective.
nodes.response: Some effective methods, such as the use of mint in herbal remedies, existed but the scientific reason for their health benefits was not understood.

nodes.misconception: There was limited access to medical care in medieval Britain.
nodes.response: Although few people were able to afford physicians, most people were able to turn to other sources of care such as that offered by hospitals, wise people or members of their own family.

nodes.misconception: Religion was the only medieval explanation for the causes of disease and illness.
nodes.response: Religion was a widespread and commonly used explanation for disease but many other theories were also used including miasma, astrology and the Theory of the Four Humours.

nodes.misconception: There was no change in medieval surgery.
nodes.response: New developments did occur, such as the use of opium as an anaesthetic and wine to use against infection, but the impact of these was limited.

nodes.misconception: Medium-fidelity prototypes are just “tidier” versions of low-fidelity ones.
nodes.response: Medium-fidelity is not about neatness - it’s about using stronger materials and semi-functional builds to test ergonomics and usability.

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense is never used in spoken German.
nodes.response: The irregular verbs 'haben' and 'sein', modal verbs and 'es gab' are all common in spoken German. Other verbs in the imperfect mainly appear in written texts.

nodes.misconception: That we will all have the same answer to a question about how a writer presents a particular character or theme.
nodes.response: The way we respond to how a writer presents a particular character or theme will be very individual since our responses depend on our own experiences or memories.

nodes.misconception: That meeting someone unknown in a strange place will always be scary.
nodes.response: Instead of feeling scared, you might also feel excited or intrigued and you can use language to have this effect on the reader.

nodes.misconception: We use 'wann' to say what we did, do or will do 'when'.
nodes.response: 'Wann' is a question word and means 'when' in questions and indirect questions. Use 'als' for 'when' when referring to specific past events or points in time and 'wenn' for repeated actions or conditions in the present or future.

nodes.misconception: 'Bei' always means 'at (the)' or 'with (the)'.
nodes.response: 'Bei' can mean 'at (the)' or 'with (the)' when followed by a noun, but it can also be used to mean 'whilst' or 'in the process of' before a nominalised infinitive.

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to form the plural in German.
nodes.response: German has several rules for forming plurals. The best way to correctly form plurals is to learn the rules, use an example for each rule as a guide, and frequently practise them. As in English, some nouns are used without plurals.

nodes.misconception: There is only one way to form the plural in German.
nodes.response: German has several rules for forming plurals. The best way to correctly form plurals is to learn the rules, use an example for each rule as a guide, and frequently practise them. As in English, some nouns are used without plurals.

nodes.misconception: All German past participles start with 'ge-'.
nodes.response: Verbs starting with inseparable prefixes like 'be-', 'er-', 'ent-' and 'ver-' do not need 'ge'. Neither do verbs ending in '-ieren', e.g., 'interessiert'. Separable prefixes appear before 'ge-' in the perfect tense, e.g., 'aufgemacht', 'eingeführt'.

nodes.misconception: All German past participlies start with 'ge-'
nodes.response: Verbs starting with inseparable prefixes like 'be-', 'er-', 'ent-' and 'ver-' do not need 'ge'. Neither do verbs ending in '-ieren', e.g., 'interessiert'. Separable prefixes appear before 'ge-' in the perfect tense, e.g., 'aufgemacht', 'eingeführt'.

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like prediction and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all listening comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as prediction and avoiding distractors are very helpful, the single most important factor in successfuly answering listening questions is having a secure knowledge of vocabulary.

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like prediction and avoiding distractors to successfully complete all listening comprehension questions
nodes.response: Whilst strategies such as prediction and avoiding distractors are very helpful, the single most important factor in successfuly answering listening questions is having a secure knowledge of vocabulary.

nodes.misconception: Possessive adjectives don't change their endings, like in English.
nodes.response: German possessive adjectives change their endings based on case and gender.

nodes.misconception: Possessive adjectives don't need endings.
nodes.response: Possessive adjectives take the same endings as 'ein'.

nodes.misconception: Only the tense of the verb can tell us whether a sentence is referring to present, past or future events.
nodes.response: Adverbs of time are also very important in helping us to identify time frames, particularly when the present tense is used for future meaning.

nodes.misconception: For verb stems ending in ‘-el’, remove the 'e' from the stem in all present tense forms.
nodes.response: For verb stems ending in ‘-el’, remove the 'e' from the stem in the first person singular of the present tense only.

nodes.misconception: 'z' is pronounced the same way in both English and German.
nodes.response: German [z] sounds like the English 'ts'. German [s-] is pronounced like the English 'z'. Use example words to remind you of the difference, e.g., 'Zug' (train) and 'Suche' (search).

nodes.misconception: You can only succeed in listening comprehension if you know all the vocabulary.
nodes.response: Whilst vocabulary knowledge is the most important element for success, other strategies can help, for example, close pre-reading of the questions, predicting vocabulary, avoiding distractors and checking answers carefully.

nodes.misconception: Developing a melody is only a feature of classical styles, not pop and rock.
nodes.response: Almost all musical styles use melodic development. Different styles use different techniques typically - in pop styles, for example, singers often develop melodies through adding melisma, extra notes and different vocal techniques.

nodes.misconception: Using new ideas in every bar is the best way to compose a melody
nodes.response: Finding a balance of repetition and variety is usually more successful as it helps the melody become memorable.

nodes.misconception: Children may not have heard of glaciers and may think that the only year-round ice is at the poles. Melting ice caps and glaciers do not affect sea level.
nodes.response: Teaching slides introduce ice caps and glaciers and note that they are found all over the world. The effect of melting ice caps and glaciers on sea level is explained and children have a chance to model it.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils can't understand that substances can change from one state to another state.
nodes.response: Ensure that the language used is solid state, liquid state and gas state, not solid, liquid and gas.

nodes.misconception: Particle spacing can be overemphasised at the expense of particle movement.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils understand that although particles can move over each other, the forces of attraction mean that the particles are touching.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that only common materials such as ice melt at room temperature or that when something melts, the liquid is a different substance to the original solid.
nodes.response: Children are shown a range of materials with different melting temperatures which range from below to above room temperature. They are taught to refer to materials in a way that highlights the fact that the material is still the same substance.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that only common materials melt at room temperature or that when something melts, the liquid is a different substance to the original solid.
nodes.response: Children are shown a range of materials with different melting temperatures, ranging from below to above room temperature. They are taught to refer to materials in a way that highlights the fact that the material is still the same substance.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that only common materials such as ice melt; that materials cannot melt at room temperature or that when something melts, the liquid is a different substance to the original solid.
nodes.response: Children are shown a range of materials with different melting temperatures which range from below to above room temperature. They are taught to refer to materials in a way that highlights the fact that the material is still the same substance.

nodes.misconception: Once menstruation starts, a female will get one period a month until they experience the menopause.
nodes.response: Most menstruating females experience between 11 - 13 menstrual cycles per year. However, pregnancy, stress, weight fluctuation, holidays and hormone changes can all disrupt cycles and therefore not everyone experiences a period ‘once a month’.

nodes.misconception: All women's health conditions are menstrual disorders.
nodes.response: Women's health conditions affect different body systems. Some mainly affect the menstrual cycle, while others affect hormones or several body systems. PMOS is an endocrine condition, although menstrual changes can be one of its symptoms.

nodes.misconception: Menstruation is dirty and shameful.
nodes.response: Anyone of any background can talk about menstruation.  Make sure people who are most affected have the space to speak for themselves.

nodes.misconception: Females are irritable during their period.
nodes.response: During the menstrual cycle, females may experience intensified emotions that can impact their mood. However, this does not make their emotions any less valid.

nodes.misconception: Some pupils may struggle to believe the impact your mindset can have on performance.
nodes.response: Your mindset can be the difference between giving up and persisting, through the use of mindfulness, visualisation and positive self talk anything is possible.

nodes.misconception: People who experience mental health conditions do so because they have not looked after themselves properly.
nodes.response: Anyone can experience mental health conditions. There are some experiences that may influence our mental health, but it is never anyone's fault.

nodes.misconception: All migrants workers settled in England to work in the wool trade.
nodes.response: Not all migrant workers settled in England to work in the wool trade. Italian bankers are an example of a migrant group who were invited to work as moneylenders, and had very little to do with the English wool trade.

nodes.misconception: Merge sort is the most efficient sorting algorithm for all cases.
nodes.response: For smaller data sets, simpler algorithms such as insertion sort or bubble sort can be faster due to the overhead in merge sort of having to break apart the data to be sorted.

nodes.misconception: Roots are not a tissue of the plant, or contain living cells, also that wood is not made of living cells.
nodes.response: Show the cells of roots and how they divide to allow the length and width of the root to grow; also the rings on trees that indicate new cell division in the trunk of a tree.

nodes.misconception: When saying what you will do in French, a separate word is needed for 'will'.
nodes.response: The simple future in French is a simple tense because it is made of one word. The idea of 'will' is created through the correct verb stem and ending. Most -er verbs use the infinitive as stem for the simple future.

nodes.misconception: All verbs use their infinitive to form the stem in the future tense.
nodes.response: There are key irregular verb stems to learn for the future tense. Confident use of these verbs will add greatly to overall accuracy and help students to express themselves confidently in the future tense.

nodes.misconception: All verbs use their infinitive to form the stem in the future tense.
nodes.response: There are key irregular verb stems to learn for the future tense. Confident use of these verbs will add greatly to overall accuracy and help students to express themselves confidently in the future tense.

nodes.misconception: Superlative sentences have the same word order in English and French.
nodes.response: Take care when writing or translating superlative sentences as the French word order differs quite significantly from English, e.g., 'the most interesting lesson' > 'the lesson the most interesting'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think floods are only destructive.
nodes.response: Explain that floodwaters can be very dangerous and cause much damage, but they also bring water and nutrients to the land for growing crops.

nodes.misconception: It is best to focus first on the unfamiliar words in a longer text.
nodes.response: This should be done in last place, when context has been read.

nodes.misconception: Like in English, we use the verb 'I am' ('je suis') with age.
nodes.response: In French, we use the verb 'I have' ('j'ai') with age, e.g. 'j'ai huit ans' - 'I am (have) eight (years)'.

nodes.misconception: All Jews reject Jesus as the Messiah.
nodes.response: There is a very small number of Jews, known as Messianic Jews, who regard Jesus as the Messiah.

nodes.misconception: Metadata is only used when a user needs to know when a file was made or changed.
nodes.response: Metadata can be used in a variety of ways. For example, software can be designed to make use of metadata for effective cataloguing and providing extra information about the properites of a file being used.

nodes.misconception: The metallic structure model is a replication of reality. Therefore, metals contain seawater. The concept of electric current is challenging. Some may think that electrons jump from atom to atom.
nodes.response: Discuss why scientists use models with the pupils, explaining that a model is only as good as what it can explain, so it develops over time. Remind pupils how an electric circuit works before discussing why metals are good conductors.

nodes.misconception: Pupils find it difficult to carry out a complex 3-stage practical.
nodes.response: Demonstrate the practical or do a 'follow with me' step-by-step method. If you are short on time you could just carry out the first part of the practical to produce the copper sulfate solution then stop.

nodes.misconception: Recycling metals reduces their quality.
nodes.response: Most metals, including aluminium and steel, can be repeatedly recycled without negatively impacting their properties.

nodes.misconception: There are exceptions for both metals and non-metals, which have different properties.
nodes.response: Use examples such as mercury and graphite in your teaching.

nodes.misconception: A metal is an individual atom. The property of a metal atom is the same as the bulk material. Pupils get confused between the attractive forces in the metal atoms and the metallic bond.
nodes.response: Reinforce the idea that atoms are tiny and not visible to the naked eye. The material we know as metal is many millions of atoms joined together. Revisit the structure of the atoms before introducing the idea of metallic bonding and giant structure.

nodes.misconception: Pressure and heating caused by burying alone is enough to cause metamorphism or rock to melt.
nodes.response: Highlight that the temperatures / pressures needed for metamorphism or rocks to melt are typically found at plate boundaries / hot spots.

nodes.misconception: Retrograde is a term only used in dance.
nodes.response: Retrograde is a term used in many artforms, it is particularly prevalent in music and films.

nodes.misconception: Projection means that you have to look up.
nodes.response: Projection is effectively communicating a dance idea. This often involves looking outwards towards an audience but would not be appropriate if communicating a concept such a secrecy, nervousness or reluctance.

nodes.misconception: That everyone in power sees education as a way to better society.
nodes.response: How does it feel when you don't understand something? Confusing? Scary? Disorientating? How could the pigs use this to their advantage?

nodes.misconception: Conversation answers should be kept as short and simple as possible.
nodes.response: It is important to develop conversation answers to showcase a range of vocabulary and grammar. This can be achieved by using adverbs to add more detail and by incorporating a range of grammatical persons.

nodes.misconception: Micro:bits can work on their own by being connected in a circuit
nodes.response: Micro:bits have to have a program downloaded before being connected into a circuit

nodes.misconception: External components must be used with microcontrollers to create control systems.
nodes.response: Microcontrollers have on board inputs and ouputs and connection points for additional external components.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that micro-organisms are very tiny animals or that they are not living things. Pupils may think that all micro-organisms are harmful germs.
nodes.response: Explain that micro-organisms are living things as they carry out the same processes as other living things, but they aren't animals because they have a simpler structure than animals. Explain that some helpful micro-organisms live inside our bodies.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that mould is a type of plant because of its colour or the way it grows.
nodes.response: Explain that plants make their own food using photosynthesis and mould does not, so it cannot be a plant. Instead, it gets its nutrients from the organic matter that it is growing on. Also, unlike plants, mould does not need light to survive or grow.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not consider mould to be a living thing because it does not move in the ways we are familiar with animals moving.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that all living things grow, reproduce and move, and that mould can do all of these things. It is a type of fungus that is a living thing and part of the micro-organisms group.

nodes.misconception: To test simple circuits, you need to create a physical representation of the circuits.
nodes.response: Like many CAD applications, Tinkercad can simulate circuit operation within the circuit workspace.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all moulds and fungi are harmful and no useful products can be extracted from them.
nodes.response: Explain that, while many moulds and fungi can be harmful to humans and other animals, many have uses in medicine such as penicillin, once they have been properly processed by scientists.

nodes.misconception: Scientific drawings made using a microscope are difficult to do and often sketched like an artwork. The requirements are clear and precise and require practise to get right.
nodes.response: The expectations for scientific drawings are clearly stated and shown visually. Opportunities to practise drawing different structures are included throughout the lesson.

nodes.misconception: Pupils expend far too much energy by sprint starting instead of finding their race pace, leading them to tire in the second half of the race.
nodes.response: Pupils should focus on finding their race pace, not getting over excited at the start line, beginning too fast or being influenced by others who do. Ideally, the second half of the race is completed quicker than the first (called a negative split).

nodes.misconception: Pupils may perform middle distances by jogging the majority to conserve energy and putting a sprint in at the end. This often leads to pupils wishing they had put more effort into the initial stages.
nodes.response: A well performed 800m requires a fine line between holding back some energy for the finish but also performing at around 80-90% maximum effort for around the first 600m.

nodes.misconception: 'Mieux' and 'plus mal/moins bien' can be used interchangeably with 'le mieux' and 'le plus mal' or ''le moins bien'.
nodes.response: 'Le mieux' and 'le plus mal'/'le moins bien' are superlative adverbs to describe actions as '(the) best' or '(the) worst'. 'Mieux' and 'moins bien'/'plus mal'  describe actions as 'better' or 'less well'/'worse' and are comparative adverbs.

nodes.misconception: The sound-symbol correspondence [ie] is always pronounced as in 'Liebe'.
nodes.response: When [ie] is the final but unstressed syllable in a word, pronounce [i] and [e] as separate vowel sounds, e.g., 'Familie'.

nodes.misconception: All migrants are refugees
nodes.response: Not all migrants are refugees; some move for economic or educational reasons. Explain the differences between refugees and other migrants.

nodes.misconception: 'Huir' works in exactly the same way as all regular -ir verbs, e.g. 'escribir'.
nodes.response: The verb 'huir' has a spelling change (i → y) in the present tense in the 1st person singular, 2nd person singular, 3rd person singular, and 3rd person plural forms: huyo, huyes, huye, huyen. This makes the vowel pronunciation easier - huyo not huio.

nodes.misconception: Modal verbs require a 'zu' before the infinitive.
nodes.response: Two-verb structures without a modal verb require 'zu' before the infinitive, e.g., 'Ich habe Lust, schwimmen zu gehen.'.

nodes.misconception: Migrant experiences were dependent solely on when they migrated to England.
nodes.response: Migrant experiences were dependent on a variety of factors, this includes when they migrated, the relationship between each migrant group and the authorities and where in England they settled.

nodes.misconception: All migration in the Middle East is forced due to conflict.
nodes.response: While war and displacement are significant in parts of the Middle East, the region is also a major destination for voluntary economic migration, especially to the Gulf States like the UAE, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia.

nodes.misconception: Migration only has negative impacts.
nodes.response: Migration also brings benefits such as skills and expertise for the jobs market, economic benefits and a more diverse society.

nodes.misconception: All migrants in the 18th and 19th centuries migrated for economic reasons and led successful lives in Britain as a result.
nodes.response: Although most migrants settled for economic reasons, the expansion of the British Empire and greater civil liberties also attracted a greater number of migrants in this period.

nodes.misconception: All Protestant migrants had entirely positive experiences.
nodes.response: Most Protestant migrants had largely positive experiences in this period, however, there are still examples of Protestants who did not maintain the support of the authorities and the Church, such as the Palatines.

nodes.misconception: All white migrants had positive experiences in the modern period.
nodes.response: Although they were often favoured by immigration laws, they still faced hostility on arriving in Britain. For example, many Irish migrants experienced the same discrimination from landlords as Caribbean migrants.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that 10 mm are larger than 1 cm.
nodes.response: There are 10 mm in 1 cm.  1 cm is made up of 10 mm.  10 mm and 1 cm are equivalent in length.

nodes.misconception: A belief that our identity is fixed and permanent.
nodes.response: Who we are and how that is expressed can be changed, and is likely to shift throughout our life. We can communicate who we are through our expression, how we dress, how we speak and by taking part in activities that are important to us.

nodes.misconception: Minimising waste means reducing the size of a product.
nodes.response: Using materials efficiently can be achieved by reducing size, but also by working accurately. This can be done by using stencils / templates, tesselation and nesting.

nodes.misconception: A scale always starts on the note do.
nodes.response: We are used to using the Solfège note names in the order - do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti, do. This is only correct for major scales. A minor scale starts on the note la.

nodes.misconception: Pupils move in the wrong direction so they are parallel instead of mirroring. When pupils perform their sequence on apparatus, they lose control, extension and flow.
nodes.response: Practise mirrored movements to create muscle memory. Pupils should adapt their sequences to work on apparatus so they don't lose quality. Pupils can also focus on communication to help improve the quality of their sequence on apparatus.

nodes.misconception: One pupil always leads so that their timing is out. Variations in angles of movement make the mirroring look uneven. Pupils move in the wrong direction so they are parallel instead of mirroring
nodes.response: Pupils should practise counting or using music to help them improve their timing. Pupils need to practise so they have identical body positions and use feedback to help improve this. Practise mirrored movements over and over to create muscle memory.

nodes.misconception: I can only use BORDER for short pieces of writing.
nodes.response: BORDER is also a very useful strategy for extended pieces of writing. Simply apply it to each paragraph separately. This will help you respond clearly and completely to each bullet point.

nodes.misconception: I can only use BORDER for short pieces of writing.
nodes.response: BORDER is also a very useful strategy for extended pieces of writing. Simply apply it to each paragraph separately. This will help you respond clearly and completely to each bullet point.

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like prediction to successfully complete listening comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Strategies like prediction can be useful, but the most important way to successfully answer listening comprehension questions is by having a broad vocabulary.

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like prediction to successfully complete listening comprehension questions.
nodes.response: Strategies like prediction can be useful, but the most important way to successfully answer listening comprehension questions is by having a broad vocabulary.

nodes.misconception: Adjectives in Spanish only ever appear after the noun.
nodes.response: Most adjectives in Spanish appear after the noun. However, some are used before it. These are called prenominal adjectives.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that drawing a graph with a broken axis is incorrect.
nodes.response: It is fine to do this (and is sometimes necessary) but it is important to acknowledge this when trying to draw conclusions from the graph.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may work out missing angles without writing out their justifications.
nodes.response: Each time a number which is not on the original diagram is used or found, an explanation should be given for where it has come from.

nodes.misconception: Evangelism always involves preaching in public.
nodes.response: Evangelism can involve preaching and public speaking, but it can also be carried out through subtle actions and living out the teachings of Jesus in everyday life.

nodes.misconception: Digital art lacks the creativity or authenticity of traditional methods.
nodes.response: Digital tools expand, rather than replace, creativity. Artists can blend hand-drawn, painted, or textured work into digital layers to achieve unique results.

nodes.misconception: Mixed media just means using any random materials together, it doesn’t really matter what you choose.
nodes.response: Mixed media is intentional. Each material or technique is chosen for a reason, either to add texture, create contrast, or express an idea or emotion. Artists think carefully about how the materials work together to enhance the artwork.

nodes.misconception: Digital tools replace traditional printmaking.
nodes.response: Digital tools enhance traditional methods by expanding creative possibilities - neither replaces the other.

nodes.misconception: Mixed media just means throwing lots of materials together.
nodes.response: Each material should have a purpose — it must add meaning or structure, not just make it look busy.

nodes.misconception: You don't need drawings in a textile project.
nodes.response: Drawing motifs and sketching developmental ideas during the initial stages in design work helps to consolidate ideas.

nodes.misconception: Artists only use paintbrushes to apply paint.
nodes.response: Artists can use a paintbrush to apply paint, but they can also use other tools, such as leaves, sticks and pinecones.

nodes.misconception: Primary colors are made by mixing other colours together.
nodes.response: Remind children that primary colours cannot be created by mixing other colours. Secondary colours are made by mixing two primary colours together. For example, blue and yellow make green.

nodes.misconception: When samples of water are added at different temperatures, some pupils add or subtract the temperatures, applying a mathematical process without appearing to think about what is happening.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to predict changes to the resulting temperature using water at a range of starting temperatures and then demonstrate each one, measuring the temperature of the resultant mixture each time.

nodes.misconception: Pupils confuse similarly sounding key terms; solute, solvent, solution, soluble, insoluble.
nodes.response: Spend time discussing ways to remember the differences, e.g. solvent has more letters = have more of it in the solution.

nodes.misconception: Pupils tend to misidentify similar looking apparatus.
nodes.response: Focus on the uses of each apparatus, highlight its distinguishing features to help pupils correctly identify apparatus.

nodes.misconception: Pupils either put too much or not enough detail into their drawings = muddled representations
nodes.response: Use the 'less is more' approach, and remind pupils to include labels - **clarity is key**. Allows for less detail and avoids any confusion.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find the concept of 'obligation' tricky to grasp.
nodes.response: Explain that obligations are things we think we should do or that should happen or that others think we should do or should happen.

nodes.misconception: Simulating in Tinkercad is exactly like physical testing.
