nodes.response: Tinkercad is excellent for digitally testing ideas, but you should always expect to make adjustments when you build the physical models.

nodes.misconception: User needs and wants are the same thing.
nodes.response: Needs are the essential features required for the product to function, while wants are additional features that aren't necessary but would enhance the product if included.

nodes.misconception: Analysis means zooming in to individual words and explaining what they mean.
nodes.response: Exploring quotations is more than just looking at individual words and offering paraphrase or synonym. Your exploration of the quotation should develop your ideas about the question, and look at dramatic methods (more than just individual words).

nodes.misconception: Looking at other essays is cheating or copying.
nodes.response: Working with model responses helps develop your critical skills in order to evaluate your own work. Using and adapting others' ideas is a great thing to do!

nodes.misconception: Robots will take all human jobs in the future.
nodes.response: Robots can sometimes replace people in certain jobs, especially when the work is dangerous, boring, or very hard for humans to do. People will still be needed to design, build and program robots.

nodes.misconception: The line on a distance time graph can go in any direction.
nodes.response: The line may be horizontal, time changing without a change in distance, but it can not be vertical. That would be a change in distance without a change in time. Additionally, our line cannot go backwards; time is always moving forwards.

nodes.misconception: A common misconception is that photosynthesis is just one simple reaction, as depicted by the word equation and balanced symbol equation.
nodes.response: This explores the idea that the word equation and balanced symbol equation are useful but very simple models of photosynthesis, and also explores a slightly more detailed two-stage model of the process.

nodes.misconception: The dominant allele is stronger than the recessive allele preventing its expression or that the recessive allele is an absence of the dominant allele, also that all genetic disorders are recessive.
nodes.response: Linking the allele to change in protein structure, showing that proteins are produced in the case of dominant and recessive alleles. Examples of dominant and recessive disorders provided.

nodes.misconception: A gamete has two alleles, Punnett square has too many alleles for gametes. Also that only four offspring are produced and therefore each will definitely have the genotype and phenotype shown.
nodes.response: Model the alleles within gametes so it is clear. Refer to half the gametes having each version, moving away from the idea of divisions of 4.

nodes.misconception: Lifestyle factors have only been considered important for a person's health in the modern period.
nodes.response: Lifestyle factors like diet have been considered important for many centuries, but before the 20th century this was often based on inaccurate ideas like the Theory of Four Humours.

nodes.misconception: Vaccinations have been made compulsory to ensure uptake in modern Britain.
nodes.response: Vaccinations have been voluntary for people to receive in modern Britain but many have been provided free of charge and their benefits promoted to encourage people.

nodes.misconception: The use of technology in modern medicine means doctors aren't very involved in making diagnoses.
nodes.response: Technology can help patients to monitor some health conditions themselves but many technologies that help diagnosis require a doctor to operate them or to interpret the information they provide.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often confuse the atomic number and mass number with regard to the number of electrons in an atom. They also can confuse the number of electrons which can be held by each shell.
nodes.response: Emphasise that the lower number (atomic number/proton number) represents the number of electrons (reference to the mass being larger can help). Practise as many electron arrangements as possible.

nodes.misconception: The dorian mode is the same as a minor scale.
nodes.response: There is a slight difference, with one different note. All of the modes are closely linked to major and minor scales, but have slightly different notes that help to create different moods.

nodes.misconception: Industries only modify products to make them cheaper.
nodes.response: Industries also improve products for better performance, sustainability, customer satisfaction, safety and compliance with regulations.

nodes.misconception: Designs are drawn on paper and then manufactured.
nodes.response: Computer Aided Design helps designers accurately draw their ideas before manufacturing them.

nodes.misconception: The shape inspector is only used to change the length or width of a shape.
nodes.response: You can use the shape inspector to customise different properties of a shape, including recolouring shapes.

nodes.misconception: Performing group routines often means some members of the group may struggle with the choreography and therefore feel self-conscious and demotivated.
nodes.response: Stress to each group the importance of adapting choreography to suit the needs of everyone in the group. For example, some pupils could perform backward rolls whilst others perform a more basic roll. Or everyone may change the skill they perform.

nodes.misconception: Children may use a range of observational methods to assess hardness, e.g. “heaviness” of the object, and if it breaks on impact (test for brittleness), neither of which are a test for hardness.
nodes.response: Be aware of using the correct vocabulary around testing for hardness. Explain that hardness is the ability to withstand pressure.

nodes.misconception: Assuming that substances like sodium chloride (NaCl) are diatomic.
nodes.response: It is very important to emphasise that only non-metals exist as monatomic or molecules.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to link a mole to number of particles.
nodes.response: Use real world examples of converting volumes / masses into number of particles so pupils become more comfortable converting between moles, number of particles particles and masses.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to link a mole to number of particles.
nodes.response: Use real world examples of converting volumes / masses into number of particles so pupils become more comfortable converting between moles, number of particles particles and masses.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that a lever gives you ‘something for nothing’ when used as a force multiplier.
nodes.response: Ask a pupil to lift an object by a particular height (say 10 cm) without a pivot, then with a pivot and a plank as a lever to compare the effort and distance moved in each case.

nodes.misconception: 'Il', 'elle', 'ils' and 'elles' only refer to people and not things. 'Il' therefore only means 'he' and 'elle' only means 'she'.
nodes.response: It is useful to keep in mind that 'il, elle' and 'ils, elles' can refer to things as well as people.  In this case, 'il, elle' means 'it' rather than 'he, she'.

nodes.misconception: Silent final consonants are always silent.
nodes.response: The liaison rule means that Silent Final Consonants are pronounced when the next word starts with a vowel sound (including silent h).

nodes.misconception: The noun 'un être', meaning 'a being', changes to 'une être' when referring to a girl or woman. 'Un être humain' changes to 'une être humaine' in the feminine.
nodes.response: The noun 'être' is masculine, even when referring to a girl or a woman. The phrase 'un être humain', 'a human being', refers to both genders.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that being healthy can be achieved through physical fitness, not taking into account anything else.
nodes.response: Explain that a range of different factors contribute to a healthy lifestyle, including eating a balanced diet, getting a good amount of sleep and taking part in activities that help our mental well being.

nodes.misconception: Monoclonal antibodies can act as a 'magic bullet' to deliver medication to certain cells.
nodes.response: The human body is complex and therapies using monoclonal antibodies have had some serious side effects. New treatments should always be treated with caution.

nodes.misconception: Monoprints should look “perfect” and repeatable, like digital prints.
nodes.response: Monoprints are valued for their unique, imperfect, and expressive qualities that cannot be exactly replicated.

nodes.misconception: It always rains during the monsoon season.
nodes.response: Explain that the rainfall intensity and frequency during the monsoon season can vary from year to year. Although it can rain every or most days, this is often a short period of intense rainfall followed by a period of dry conditions.

nodes.misconception: Monsters in myths and films are always portrayed as evil.
nodes.response: Monsters in myths and films are not always portrayed as evil. Creating monsters can involve using different features that portray a friendly or approachable character.

nodes.misconception: [ai] and [é] sound the same in French.
nodes.response: In some regional accents  [ai] and [é] can sound similar.  Officially there is a difference in pronunciation and meaning as the ending of the imperfect tense is supposed to be pronounced [ai], whereas a common ending of the past participle is [é].

nodes.misconception: You can use a time phrase to show whether you mean a completed action in the past or a regular past event/activity.
nodes.response: In French, the verb alone already shows whether you mean a completed action in the past (use the formation rule for the perfect tense) or a regular past event/activity (use the formation rule for the imperfect tense). Time phrases can also be added.

nodes.misconception: A subject pronoun or noun is always required when using a verb in French.
nodes.response: When using the imperative, neither subject pronoun nor noun is required. Match the spelling of the verb to the person or people who are being instructed.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think they personally can't do anything to prevent animals becoming endangered/extinct.
nodes.response: Use the resources to explain the things pupils can do to help, and encourage them to think specifically about which are possible for them.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that old discovered objects, like bits of pottery, coins and jewellery are fossils.  They also may believe that the fossil is always the actual plant or animal itself.
nodes.response: Being clear that only things that have been alive may become fossils, and not all living things are fossilised.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that human development milestones happen at the same time for everyone.
nodes.response: Using the lesson resources to support, explain that humans are all different and so grow and develop at different rates. This is why we need surveys to find out more information, as one rule cannot be applied to all humans.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that plants can decide or choose to grow in whatever way they think is best.
nodes.response: Explain that plant adaptations are inherited characteristics and the plant does not have any choice or understanding of its adaptations.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not know how humans use different senses to stay safe.
nodes.response: Examples of different scenarios where humans use different senses to check for danger and to stay safe.

nodes.misconception: A lot of people think we only touch with our hands rather than our skin. Also, that we only ever use one sense at a time.
nodes.response: Examples including touching with other parts of the body such as feet, or touching an arm against a cold metal table leg and feeling the difference in temperature.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that all the food we eat is used by the body.
nodes.response: When pupils model the lower part of the digestive system they will see some of the food is absorbed as nutrients and other parts form waste which leaves the body.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the Sun is a planet.
nodes.response: Explain that the Sun is a star because, like other stars, it is a huge ball of glowing gas which has planets travelling around it.

nodes.misconception: Mistakes with partial products are even more common where algebraic terms in the binomials have coefficients greater than 1. It is common to find pupils writing that the product of 2x and 3x is 5x
nodes.response: Reminding pupils that because multiplication is commutative the product of 2x and 3x can be thought of as 2 × 3 × x × x

nodes.misconception: You can use the same verbalisation in compound time as simple time signatures.
nodes.response: This will create problems, because there are 3 quavers in each beat in compound time. The counting method in compound time avoids confusion by ensuring there are three quavers in each beat.

nodes.misconception: All bubbles produced contain air and that it is a reversible change.
nodes.response: Teaching slides explain that the bubbles produced when acids react with bicarbonate of soda contain carbon dioxide and that this change is irreversible as a new material is produced.

nodes.misconception: Changes in state and dissolving and mixing are not reversible processes.
nodes.response: Teaching slides will show which processes can be used to reverse state changes and dissolving.  This will be explored and embedded during the practice tasks.

nodes.misconception: May consider the size of objects when comparing rather than the numerosity of the group.
nodes.response: Ensure any groups compared throughout the day are very obviously different before comparing more small things with fewer large things.

nodes.misconception: There are just two words for 'the': a masculine and feminine version.
nodes.response: There are four different ways to say 'the' in French: 'le', 'las', 'les' and 'l'' (masculine singular, feminine singular, plural and preceding a vowel/h).

nodes.misconception: The pronouns 'il' and 'elle' can only mean 'he' and 'she' in French.
nodes.response: The pronouns 'il' and 'elle' mean 'he' and 'she', they can also be translated as 'it' as all noun have a gender in French.

nodes.misconception: There is one form of the possessive adjective 'my' in French, as in English.
nodes.response: There are two forms of the possessive adjective 'my' in French: 'mon' (masculine) and 'ma' (feminine).

nodes.misconception: Motifs and symbols are the same.
nodes.response: A motif is a recurring image whereas a symbol is one thing that represents something else.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often apply equations incorrectly or do not spot obvious errors when using them due to not thinking about the science.
nodes.response: Ask pupils to describe what happens for each example in relation to their answers to problems set.

nodes.response: Ask pupils to describe what happens for each example in relation to their answers to problems set.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may find it challenging to come up with suitable motions.
nodes.response: Pupils could work in small groups for this task. As a class, come up with some ideas of what you might change or discuss related to the different aspects and have these visible for children when coming up with their motions.

nodes.misconception: Simply changing the instrument makes a leitmotif change mood.
nodes.response: While it does have an impact, changing other elements can make this even greater. Harmony, rhythm, dynamics, articulation and tempo are particularly useful for motivic transformation.

nodes.misconception: All motors operate in the same way.
nodes.response: DC motors use open-loop systems, and servo motors use a closed-loop system.

nodes.misconception: A common misconception is that castles only had a military function.
nodes.response: However, castles also had a psychological impact on the people of England. They served as a permanent reminder to the English of a foreign occupier in their land. They were also centres of administration.

nodes.misconception: Pupils assume that it is warmer at the summit of a mountain because you are 'closer to the sun'.
nodes.response: There is low pressure at altitude which means that air is thinner at the summit of a mountain. The thin air causes the cold temperatures.

nodes.misconception: The audience are always directly facing the stage/performers.
nodes.response: Whilst most theatres use an 'end on' arrangement, this isn't always the case. Fashion shows traditionally use a 'thrust' stage, lecture-demonstrations might use 'in the round' and performances such as Mummers' plays, may use 'promenade'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may miscount the squares when moving the shape, leading to inaccurate placement.
nodes.response: Encourage students to carefully count squares from the current position of each vertex and ensure consistency in their counting across the entire shape. Practice counting out loud as a class or in pairs. Relate it to counting on using a number line.

nodes.misconception: Detailed and complex 3D models are always created from scratch and therefore take a long time to create.
nodes.response: 3D models usually start off by using, adding and modifying simple 3D shapes. Further detail and complexities are then added to increase the realism of the model.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that sport and physical activity is all about competing and winning.
nodes.response: Moving and exercising is an important part of daily life, not just for organised competition. Exercising can be done for fun and is important to help our bodies and minds to stay healthy.

nodes.misconception: Perfect balance means not moving at all.
nodes.response: Balance is actually a constant series of tiny corrections. Your brain and muscles are in a non-stop conversation, making micro-adjustments to keep your centre of gravity over your base. This happens in static and dynamic balances.

nodes.misconception: Focus on pushing off from the ground with maximum force for height or distance and prioritising speed of execution.
nodes.response: The most critical skill for precision, confidence and long term athletic health is the ability to efficiently absorb and redirect force upon landing. A powerful jump with a weak or uncontrolled landing risks injury.

nodes.misconception: You are either naturally good at movement skills and sports, or you aren't.
nodes.response: Movement skills are learned and trained, just like maths and music. You need to practice and refine your technique to improve confidence and remember that growth spurts will temporarily affect coordination and this is perfectly normal.

nodes.misconception: Being good at sport just means being fast or strong.
nodes.response: Success in sport depends on coordination and balance, timing and decision making, technique and skill execution, awareness of space and teammates, and many other factors including experience. Many of these can be practised away from the sports pitch.

nodes.misconception: Struggling with coordination means you are clumsy, careless or simply not trying.
nodes.response: During adolescence, rapid growth spurts cause a temporary mismatch as limbs are longer than the brain thinks they are, which causes a calibration error. Consequently, it is essential to keep practising fine and gross motor skills as you grow.

nodes.misconception: Throwing something with more force will make it more accurate.
nodes.response: Increased force usually reduces accuracy unless the technique is correct (stance, grip, arm swing and follow through).

nodes.misconception: Pupils think the chest pass is only used for shorter distances.
nodes.response: The chest pass is a very versatile technique that can be used for short and longer distances. It works well as a technique to pass when aiming for the space a teammate is moving into.

nodes.misconception: The only way to gain MA is by increasing the input force.
nodes.response: MA can be increased by increasing the distance from the fulcrum and the effort. For example, increasing the arm length on the handle of a flat head screwdriver when opening a can of paint.

nodes.misconception: Pupils make a big touch so they don't have close control of the ball. Pupils slow down after turning with the ball.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to keep the ball close to the body so they have control at all times. Pupils should explode after the turn pushing off with their standing leg.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often dribble with their head down, focusing too much on the ball and not on teammates, spaces to move into or defenders within the space.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to develop the habit of looking up regularly to scan the area.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that muscles can push bones (when in fact they can only pull).
nodes.response: The lesson makes clear that muscles can only pull bones, and work in antagonistic pairs to pull bones in opposite directions.

nodes.misconception: Histograms with unequal bar widths are plotted against the frequency and/or pupils read the frequency density as the frequency of the class width.
nodes.response: Show what a histogram with unequal bar widths looks like when plotted against frequency. This visual aid will show pupils the distribution of data is difficult to see.

nodes.misconception: You can't prepare in advance for a discussion.
nodes.response: Developing an effective strategy and learning some phrases, will enable you to take part in discussions successfully and confidently. These can help you feel more prepared in discussion scenarios.

nodes.misconception: Magnetic field effects are often mistaken for electric field effects.
nodes.response: Be explicit in teaching that electric charges and charged objects are not magnetic.

nodes.misconception: Mistakes with the definitions of diffusion, osmosis and active transport are common, as are their application to biological scenarios.
nodes.response: The definitions are clearly stated and contextualised using key human biological processes and examples.

nodes.misconception: Balance is something you just need in gymnastics.
nodes.response: Balance is needed in many everyday activities and across many different sports.

nodes.misconception: You need to go for a run or go to the gym to develop your aerobic fitness.
nodes.response: You can improve your aerobic fitness wherever you are, with little to no equipment.

nodes.misconception: Strength training can only be done in a gym or fitness suite.
nodes.response: Strength training can easily be completed at home with different resources.

nodes.misconception: You're either a flexible person or you're not.
nodes.response: Everyone can improve their range of movement with a commitment to some stretching and flexibility training.

nodes.misconception: Jumping just requires the use of our legs.
nodes.response: To be able to jump far, you must use your legs and arms together.

nodes.misconception: Pupils confuse dribbling with simply kicking the ball away, believing that any contact with the ball is dribbling.
nodes.response: Emphasise the importance of soft, controlled touches with the inside of their feet.

nodes.misconception: Some people have the view that they are local people and new arrivals are not welcome.
nodes.response: In reality, everyone in the UK is descended from new arrivals into the UK from outside. Few people are linked to a place for a long period.

nodes.misconception: Any quotation that supports your argument can be used.
nodes.response: Select a quotation from learning cycle 1, such as "it wasn't like a man" and ask how much pupils could say about the quotation.

nodes.misconception: Hyde is solely presented as a dangerous character from the start to the end of the novella.
nodes.response: Through the character of Hyde, and others' interactions with him, we can explore Stevenson's wider cautionary message.

nodes.misconception: That the dream is only caused by Utterson being in a state of distress.
nodes.response: Unpick the details of the dream to show the parallels with the plot.

nodes.misconception: Mughal authority collapsed in the 17th century.
nodes.response: Mughal rule faced challenges, but the emperors still had enough military power and political control to maintain their authority during the 17th century.

nodes.misconception: Violence was not important during the reign of some monarchs such as Akbar the Great.
nodes.response: Violence was consistently part of the reigns of Mughal emperors. Akbar ordered the massacre of 30 000 people living in Mewar after they resisted the Mughal army in 1568.

nodes.misconception: The Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) was the founder of Islam.
nodes.response: The Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) was messenger sent to deliver the message of Islam.

nodes.misconception: There are only two types of cell: plant and animal.
nodes.response: The lesson explores the cells of unicellular organisms and some of their adaptations.

nodes.misconception: Pretending to be an object is drama, not dance.
nodes.response: Pretending to be an object is often categorised as 'physical theatre'. This is where dance and drama overlap and it draws upon skills from both disciplines. A similar connection is made when dancers represent characters or scenes from a story.

nodes.misconception: Proofs have to be solely algebraic and do not involve diagrams.
nodes.response: Proofs involve showing that a conjecture holds for multiple cases (general case). A diagram can represent multiple cases.

nodes.misconception: One object can only cast one shadow.
nodes.response: Children will investigate how the number of light sources affects the number of shadows cast by an object.

nodes.misconception: The number of spaces to translate a shape can be worked out by counting the squares on the grid.
nodes.response: If there are axes, then it is important to check the scales. The length of one square does not always represent one unit.

nodes.misconception: A negative exponent implies that the entire value is negative.
nodes.response: Refer back to the table showing the structure of how the negative exponents occur and highlight that none of the decimal values are negative.

nodes.misconception: Pupils lack fluency in pairs for 10 and so struggle to connect this to 2-digit numbers.
nodes.response: Promote fluency through games and chants and consider providing a scaffold of pairs for 10 which will help pupils develop automaticity

nodes.misconception: When working with counters students may count them and not appreciate they represent negatives.
nodes.response: Stress the importance of 2 different coloured counters as there is a need to represent positive and negative integers differently.

nodes.misconception: Using the phrase '2 negatives make a positive'.
nodes.response: Ensuring pupils understand the structure of the maths and not 'tricks' is so important. Encourage the use of correct language at all times

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not simplify after multiplying surds.
nodes.response: Surds should always be written in their simplest form for the final answer.

nodes.misconception: A reflection of a vector in the x or y axis is not the reverse of a vector.  This is often seen with equilateral triangles and vectors.
nodes.response: When multiplying the vectors by -1 this gives the opposite direction of the vector only.  The magnitude remains the same.  Investigate with pupils by drawing column vectors and multiply by -1 and compare.

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly drawing or interpreting the scales on axes.
nodes.response: Use the approach where pupils count the number of intervals of the scale and divide the difference between the intervals. For example, if there are 5 intervals and the difference is between 20 and 30, they divide 10 by 2, so each interval is 2

nodes.misconception: Rather than learning to rearrange multiplicative relationships pupils can just learn the rearrangements or use a trick.
nodes.response: There are many situations in school and out where this skill is valuable and understanding how to manipulate these relationships will help pupils to understand the mathematics rather than just learn a set of procedures or lots of formulae.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that the π symbol represents a variable, similar to letters such as r and d.
nodes.response: Reiterate the difference between variables and constants. Explain that while the radius may differ between circles, π is always the same.

nodes.misconception: Only seeing multiplication as repeated addition leads to incorrect additive strategies for ratios.
nodes.response: Focus on the multiplicative relationships between parts to whole or whole to parts. Ratios allow the multiplicative relationship to be seen.

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly drawing a scaled axis is common.
nodes.response: Use the approach where pupils count the number of intervals of the scale and divide the difference bewteen the intervals. For example, if there are 5 intervals and the difference is between 20 and 30, they divide 10 by 2, so each interval is 2

nodes.misconception: Using additive strategies instead of multiplicative.
nodes.response: Emphasise that proportional relationships maintain a constant multiplier so we are looking for a multiplicative relationship.

nodes.misconception: The short multiplication algorithm may not be correctly aligned.
nodes.response: Check that the decimal point aligns in the decimal fraction and the product. Scaffolding with place value columns may support further.

nodes.misconception: Children may scale the decimal fraction inaccurately or may forget to scale the product accordingly to solve the original equation.
nodes.response: If a decimal fraction has only tenths, we multiply by 10 to form a whole number. If the decimal fraction has hundredths, we multiply by 100 to form a whole number.  Remember to adjust the product to answer the original equation.

nodes.misconception: When using the expanded method, pupils may not align the digits correctly with the same place value.
nodes.response: Use clear teacher modelling and continue to ask what each digit that has been recorded represents and link back to the place value chart.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not align or regroup correctly leading to an inaccurate calculation.
nodes.response: Model accurately what happens when we regroup from 10s to 100s. Why did this happen? How do we record this?

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not align or regroup correctly leading to an inaccurate calculation.
nodes.response: Continue to ask what each digit that has been recorded represents. Demonstrate the regrouping using base ten blocks to help.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not regroup correctly if they do not understand the place value of digits in a factor.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use the stem sentences / array to identify when they may need to regroup.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not regroup correctly.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use the stem sentences / array to identify when they may need to regroup.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not record partitioned factors as tens and ones leading to incorrect calculation.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to use the stem sentences to support their thinking. Use the language of ___ tens to support place value.

nodes.misconception: When using the short method, pupils may not align the digits correctly with the same place value.
nodes.response: Continue to ask what each digit that has been recorded represents, linking back to the place value chart.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not align or regroup correctly leading to an inaccurate calculation.
nodes.response: Reiterate that if the product of the single digit and the tens number is greater than 100 then you regroup ten tens into one hundred.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not align or regroup correctly leading to an inaccurate calculation.
nodes.response: Ask children about the additional ten or tens as a small digit to be added in with the tens. What does this show? What is the value?

nodes.misconception: Pupils may partition numbers incorrectly and arrange grid model incorrectly.
nodes.response: Clear teacher modelling, ask pupils 'what does this digit represent?'

nodes.misconception: Incorrectly regrouping or forgetting to record a regrouped amount.
nodes.response: Clear teacher modelling. 'What does this digit represent?' 'Where do we place the regrouped amount?'

nodes.misconception: Misalignment of digits when setting out short multiplication.
nodes.response: Clear teacher modelling, ask pupils 'what does this digit represent?' Return to expanded layout briefly, before re-doing the problem.

nodes.misconception: Children may misalign digits when arranging into the short multiplication layout.
nodes.response: Children should use unitising language to help them understand and apply this to formal written methods.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may look to calculate each expression straight away.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are encouraged to estimate expressions, showing how this can be more efficient particularly when looking to compare expressions. The product is not always needed.

nodes.misconception: Pupils find it difficult to represent the problem as an expression or equation as they misinterpret what the whole is.
nodes.response: Draw attention to what the whole is in each example. You might like to build up each image with a whole at a time, describing the fraction of the whole that is shaded/represented.

nodes.misconception: Pupils resort to a procedure with little understanding for how we convert between improper fractions and mixed numbers.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to make connections between improper fractions and mixed numbers using both area models and number lines. Focus on reasoning by manipulating parts to complete wholes and where the wholes and parts are represented on the number line.

nodes.misconception: Pupils multiply both the numerator and denominator by the whole number.
nodes.response: Ensure pupils are given time to explore how equations are represented using multiple representations and avoiding 'finding the answer' initially. Encourage children to reason how each equation is linked to the representations.

nodes.misconception: Pupils struggle to identify how much the rod has been scaled by as they cannot visualise the fractional size of the new whole.
nodes.response: Encourage pupils to visualise how much the whole has shrunk by. Avoid pupils using the rods to immediately  find out what size of the new whole, encourage pupils to visualise and estimate prior to checking with the rods.

nodes.misconception: Children may get confused with the vocabulary when we say, for example, zero point one two rather than zero point twelve. They may also confuse how we write, for example, 32 hundredths.
nodes.response: We say zero point one two to show that there is one tenth and two hundredths. 32 hundredths is composed of 30 hundredths - this is the same as 3 tenths and we have 2 more hundredths so 32 hundredths is written 0.32

nodes.misconception: Children may incorrectly write the amount of tenths e.g. 49 tenths may be written as 0.49
nodes.response: There are ten tenths in one whole. So e.g. 49 tenths is composed of 4 ones and 9 more tenths. We write this as 4.9

nodes.misconception: 3(y+2) expands to 3y+2.
nodes.response: 3 lots of 12 isn't 3x10+2 so 3 lots of (y+2) isn't 3y+2. Get students to draw this out. To visualise it.

nodes.misconception: How to deal with exponents. y^2 times by y makes 3y. Or at least has a coefficient that is not 1.
nodes.response: Unsimplifying first. Not sure? Break it down. What is it? a^2 is a x a. So a^2 x a must be a x a x a.

nodes.misconception: Children may 'add' a zero when multiplying or vice versa when dividing. Children may place a zero at the end of the decimal fraction when multiplying, or vice versa when dividing.
nodes.response: When we 'add' zero, the value of the number does not change. When we multiply or divide by a power of 10, we need to move all the digits the appropriate spaces to the left/right even if this means bridging one and moving into the decimal places.

nodes.misconception: Children may confuse use of the Base 10 equipment. They may also confuse the equivalence between dividing by 10/100/1,000 and multiplying by 0.1/0.01/0.001.
nodes.response: The large cube now represents one whole. The smaller blocks represent decimal fraction numbers. Use stem sentences to support common mistakes: when a number is divided by ___, it is the same as multiplying by ___

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think 5(y+1)-2(y+3) = 5y+5-2y+6
nodes.response: Correct use of the distributive law with either algebra tiles or an area model will demonstrate why this is wrong.

nodes.misconception: When multiplying terms with coefficients, pupils also add the coefficients as well as the exponents.
nodes.response: Pupils should be encouraged to rewrite their expression using the associative and commutative laws, with the number parts grouped and powers grouped. This hopefully avoids this error as they can see it is the product of the numbers.

nodes.misconception: When pupils multiply decimals, they use the column method and align the decimal points.
nodes.response: If the column method is used, encourage integer multiplication and use of powers of 10 to adjust the answer to the original calculation.

nodes.misconception: Students may misinterpret Murakami's semantic field and assume the text is a horror, mystery or thriller story.
nodes.response: If you really break down Murakami's use of semantic field, his word choice is more centered around dynamism of a living organism.

nodes.misconception: Hindus worship images and murtis.
nodes.response: Hindus use murtis and images to focus their worship or to align with the energy of a murti.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may believe that the results from a few children they measured can be applied to all humans.
nodes.response: Share each group's results and see how they are different. Explain that a much larger sample may provide different results.

nodes.misconception: Students may think if you have big muscles you are strong, if you have small muscles you are weak.
nodes.response: Show images to illustrate a runner may be very lean and a weightlifter may have huge muscles, but both are strong, just in different ways.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that there is just one huge muscle that moves the body.
nodes.response: Use diagrams that explain how muscles work in pairs and that muscles are different sizes throughout the body.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that muscles are only found attached to the skeleton to move our limbs, and nowhere else.
nodes.response: Discussion of three types of muscle, where they are found, and their roles.

nodes.misconception: Connected circuits will always work.
nodes.response: Circuits need to be checked that the connections are accurate and the components all work.

nodes.misconception: Museum galleries only contain paintings.
nodes.response: Museum galleries display a range of artefacts which include paintings and other physical objects.

nodes.misconception: Museum galleries are not organised in any order. Artefacts are displayed randomly.
nodes.response: Museum galleries are carefully designed and include thought about access and display of artefacts.

nodes.misconception: Pupils often think that a mushroom is a plant.
nodes.response: Explain to pupils that mushrooms are not plants (or animals), rather they are the fruit bodies of a group of micro-organisms called fungi (singular fungus).

nodes.misconception: I should use my throat to start a note.
nodes.response: Using the throat creates a tight, harsh sound. To create a clear, controlled tone, we should use a singing breath to initiate the sound, pushing the sound from our bellies.

nodes.misconception: Most music in the Baroque, Classical and Romantic periods was written for an orchestra.
nodes.response: Although a lot of the most famous music now is orchestral, it was much more diverse than this - composers wrote for many different ensembles, large and small. These included solo compositions, duets, trios, quartets, quintets and many others.

nodes.misconception: Like in English, pronouns are needed with verbs to know who the verb refers to.
nodes.response: Pronouns are not often necessary in Spanish. Verb endings change to indicate the person who the verb refers to.

nodes.misconception: Contrast means the sections don't need to relate to each other.
nodes.response: Contrasting sections should still share something (an instrument, a rhythm, a key) to feel part of the same piece.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that pulse and rhythm are the same thing.
nodes.response: Explain that pulse is the steady, consistent beat that runs through the music and rhythm is the pattern of sounds.

nodes.misconception: Islam supports violence in response to conflict.
nodes.response: Islam teaches that violence is only allowed in self-defence and under strict conditions.

nodes.misconception: Islam teaches that all crimes are equally wrong.
nodes.response: Islam teaches that crimes should be judged fairly, based on harm, intention and context. Serious crimes like murder are treated more severely, while causes like poverty or illness may affect how a crime is viewed.

nodes.misconception: In Islam, justice is always focused on punishment.
nodes.response: Islam teaches justice must be fair and include mercy. Offenders who repent can be forgiven. It's about responsibility and change, not just punishment.

nodes.misconception: Being a religion based on peace means that everybody will be pacifist.
nodes.response: Religious believers interpret scripture in different ways and will make individual decisions based on personal worldviews.

nodes.misconception: The Muslim creation story is exactly the same as stories told by Jews and Christians.
nodes.response: There are some similar ideas about creation and some differences.

nodes.misconception: Animals are just for humans to use as they wish.
nodes.response: The Prophet Muhammad taught that we should be kind to all animals.

nodes.misconception: Islam teaches that people are born sinful or evil.
nodes.response: Islam teaches that all people are born pure (in a state of fitrah), and have the ability to choose between right and wrong.

nodes.misconception: Halal and haram just applies to food and dietary laws.
nodes.response: Anything that is acceptable or forbidden in Islam is known as halal and haram.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that bacteria are not living organisms and/or do not evolve. Pupils may also think that all bacteria are harmful.
nodes.response: The lesson explores two examples of evolution in bacteria, explaining each example through mutation, reproduction and natural selection.

nodes.misconception: Mixing up amino acids and nucleotides, also nucleotides and bases.
nodes.response: Activity checks: Nucleotides contain a base; DNA is a polymer of nucleotides that codes for the order of amino acids in a protein.

nodes.misconception: Respect means you have to believe the same things as others.
nodes.response: Respect means listening and valuing others, even if your beliefs are different.

nodes.misconception: Our boundaries don't apply to people we know well.
nodes.response: Everyone should respect our personal boundaries, even people we know well, like family and friends.

nodes.misconception: Healthy eating restricts treats.
nodes.response: A balanced diet can include occasional treats in moderation alongside nutritious foods.

nodes.misconception: A performance needs to be on a stage, at a theatre.
nodes.response: Performing is where we show our work to another, it might be on a stage, but equally it can be a part of the lesson where we share ideas, thoughts and opinions so that we can all improve.

nodes.misconception: 'Avoir' always means 'to have/having'.
nodes.response: Most of the time, we translate 'avoir' as 'to have/having' but there are expressions, where we would use the verb to be in English, where French uses 'avoir', usually expressing feelings/states e.g 'avoir froid', to be cold.

nodes.misconception: Knowing the lower numbers is enough to be able to tell the time in French.
nodes.response: As French uses 24-hour clock more than English and gives the minutes after the hour, you need to know numbers 1-59 well.

nodes.misconception: Most people have enough fruit and vegetables in their diet.
nodes.response: Most people need to eat more fruit and vegetables. We need at least 5 A DAY.

nodes.misconception: Spanish doesn't use the definite article 'the' when describing facial features.
nodes.response: In Spanish, the definite article 'the' is needed when describing facial features, e.g. 'tiene los ojos azules y la nariz pequeña'. In English, with plural features the article is omitted, e.g. 'she has blue eyes', or replaced by a/an; 'a small nose'.

nodes.misconception: The preposition 'à' has only one translation in English: at.
nodes.response: The preposition 'à' has in fact different meanings in English, it can be translated as at, in or to.

nodes.misconception: The SSC [s] always sounds like the English 'z'.
nodes.response: The SSC [s] sounds 'hard' (like the English 'z') when it is between two vowels. It sounds 'soft' at the beginning of a word/syllable, before or after a consonant and when there is a double [ss].

nodes.misconception: Children have complete control over what they eat.
nodes.response: Many children will have little control over their meal choices, so focus on awareness and try to highlight the areas where they might have control, such as what they may choose for lunch at school.

nodes.misconception: Like in English, adjectives do not change spelling based on the number of the noun described: a blue book - some blue books.
nodes.response: Unlike in English, adjectives change spelling based on the number (and gender) of the noun they describe: un livre bleu - des livres bleus.

nodes.misconception: A diet means to lose weight.
nodes.response: The word ‘diet’ describes all the food and drink we consume.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that when performing mirroring duets they should remain on the spot.
nodes.response: Mirroring duets typically remain in situ (and may need to for safety reasons e.g. in a small space), but they should be encouraged to lean towards or away from their partner, as well as move sideways to prevent the work from becoming purely gestural.

nodes.misconception: Your fitness is fixed and cannot be changed.
nodes.response: Fitness can improve slowly and over time. Measuring our fitness only tells us what we can do on that day.

nodes.misconception: If a relationship is positive, it will always be positive.
nodes.response: In order for a relationship to remain positive, we have to be proactive and make conscious choices to keep the relationship positive.

nodes.misconception: The possessive adjectives 'my' - mi - and 'your' - tu - stay the same for both singular and plural nouns as they do in English.
nodes.response: In Spanish, the possessive adjectives change for singular and plural nouns; 'mi' becomes 'mis' and 'tu' becomes 'tus' before plural nouns.

nodes.misconception: Singing louder means the children are more engaged and singing better.
nodes.response: For children to develop sound intonation and accuracy, they need to sing gently and not be encouraged to always sing loudly.

nodes.misconception: Pupils think that in order to bring graffiti 'tags' to life through movement, you have to write in the air.
nodes.response: Creating a 'tag' using your body can involve writing in the air, but it could also include making and holding a shape, or even using the colour, style or shading as the stimulus for your actions.

nodes.misconception: Plural adjectival nouns always end in '-en'.
nodes.response: All plural adjectival nouns preceded by 'die' and all in the dative end in '-en', but for plural adjectival nouns without articles, use '-e' in the nominative and accusative.

nodes.misconception: Question words can replace definite articles as relative pronouns in relative clauses.
nodes.response: Question words, such as 'wo', can be used as pronouns in relative clauses, but they should not be used to translate 'who' or 'which' when adding information about the noun in the main clause.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that only four-legged mammals that are pets, are animals.
nodes.response: Discuss a range of familiar animals that can be kept as pets that are not just four-legged.

nodes.misconception: Students often forget to change the non-metal name to either -ide or -ate.
nodes.response: Emphasise when the non-metal reacts with a metal it changes its name to -ide. It is -ate if the non-metal is also bonded to oxygen.

nodes.misconception: Everything that lives in water is a fish and that fish cannot breathe underwater.
nodes.response: Examples of fish and amphibians with explanation that both can live in water. Explanation that fish use gills to breathe underwater.

nodes.misconception: Pupils might think all nanoparticles are hazardous without considering their varied applications and benefits.
nodes.response: Clarify that while nanoparticles may pose risks, they also offer significant benefits in medicine, technology, and environmental protection, with risks varying by type and usage.

nodes.misconception: Sait-Domingue was independent from France under Toussaint L'Ouverture's leadership
nodes.response: Toussaint L'Ouverture was technically the French Governor of Saint-Domingue due to his leadership during the slave uprising there during the 1790s. His attempt to establish the colony as a free country though in 1801 was a step too far for Napoleon.

nodes.misconception: If a verb is 'strong', its past participle always has a vowel change.
nodes.response: In German, a strong verb has a stem change in one or more tenses. Some strong verbs have a stem change in the present tense but not in the perfect tense, e.g., 'sehen' - 'er, sie, es sieht' - 'hat gesehen'.

nodes.misconception: 'Sie' always means 'she'.
nodes.response: As a subject pronoun, 'sie' can mean 'she' or 'they'. As an object pronoun, 'sie' means 'her' or 'it'.

nodes.misconception: The Inspector can only be interpreted as representing absolute truth, as he always speaks with authority and moral certainty.
nodes.response: The Inspector may not represent absolute truth. He selectively reveals information and uses moral rhetoric, which could suggest he's guiding the audience toward a particular interpretation of events.

nodes.misconception: The narrative voice of 'Animal Farm' reports the truth to the reader.
nodes.response: Arguably, the narrative voice withholds information about the pig's oppressive behaviour.

nodes.misconception: Narrow actions are always vertical. Pupils perform gymnastics actions in silence to be well-behaved. Pupils show empathy to others only by saying that they like their movements and balances.
nodes.response: Narrow actions can be vertical or horizontal. Pupils perform gymnastics actions in silence to show good control. Encourage pupils to say why they liked others' gymnastics and to suggest improvements or new ideas by communicating kindly with respect.

nodes.misconception: Students may believe that there was only rationing in Britain during WW2.
nodes.response: Rationing continued until 1954.

nodes.misconception: Climate change is only caused by human activity.
nodes.response: Human activity has been significant in recent climate change, but natural factors have caused changes to the climate over millions of years.

nodes.misconception: Natural forms are always perfectly symmetrical, like leaves or flowers.
nodes.response: While some natural forms show symmetry, most have irregular, flowing shapes. Even symmetrical forms often have variations, this is part of what makes nature interesting to artists.

nodes.misconception: Graphic design is mostly digital, so nature isn’t really relevant.
nodes.response: Graphic design often draws from organic, natural inspiration - many professional designs use textures, forms, and concepts from nature to create emotional or symbolic meaning.

nodes.misconception: Natural forms are always perfectly symmetrical, like leaves or flowers.
nodes.response: While some natural forms show symmetry, most have irregular, flowing shapes. Even symmetrical forms often have variations, this is part of what makes nature interesting to photographers.

nodes.misconception: Natural forms are always perfectly symmetrical, like leaves or flowers.
nodes.response: While some natural forms show symmetry, most have irregular, flowing shapes. Even symmetrical forms often have variations, this is part of what makes nature interesting to artists.

nodes.misconception: Thinking that DNA is made of a single polymer chain.
nodes.response: Use the slides and a model to reinforce that DNA contains two polymer chains in a double helix structure.

nodes.misconception: All Middle Eastern countries are rich because they have oil.
nodes.response: While oil is a major resource, not every country has it. Countries like Yemen and Jordan have little or no oil, which affects their economies differently.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not fully appreciate the wide range of landscapes, physical features and biomes in Africa.
nodes.response: Spend some time exploring different countries and regions, including major cities and different types of biome.

nodes.misconception: Many students write that organisms change themselves to become better adapted to their environment.
nodes.response: This lesson contains checks for this misconception and challenges it with examples of natural selection explained at the genetic level.

nodes.misconception: Students often think that advantageous traits are due to an organism choosing to change itself in order to be successful.
nodes.response: This lesson uses CfUs in order to explore and deconstruct this misconception.

nodes.misconception: Naturalism and expressionism are too different and cannot be used together in the same play.
nodes.response: Arguably, Priestley blends both styles. Naturalism makes the setting realistic, while expressionism distorts reality to highlight emotional and symbolic themes, strengthening his political message.

nodes.misconception: There are no new ways to be inspired by nature.
nodes.response: We can all find new things that inspire us in the world around us.

nodes.misconception: All Christian weddings are the same.
nodes.response: Christian weddings will vary depending on denomination, cultural/family traditions, etc.

nodes.misconception: Angels are male (e.g., Jibreel is male).
nodes.response: In Islam, angels are genderless but can appear in a male form.

nodes.misconception: The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are three separate gods.
nodes.response: Most Christians believe in the Oneness of God and that all three Persons of the Trinity are present in only one God, therefore the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are not three separate gods.

nodes.misconception: Only complex images or shapes can create associations.
nodes.response: Simple images or shapes can create associations to themes or ideas.

nodes.misconception: Blaming others for mistakes and rushing rather than planning first and taking care over the approach.
nodes.response: Less overall time is lost if you invest in planning, negotiating and caring for each other.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may assume that all concentration camps in this period were death camps like Auschwitz.
nodes.response: Emphasise that early camps (1933–1939) were brutal prisons for political opponents and ‘undesirables’, but were not yet part of a systematic extermination programme. The Holocaust’s industrial death camps came later.

nodes.misconception: Nazi antisemitism meant they were immediately violent towards Jews.
nodes.response: Open violence as a part of Nazi persecution only became common in 1938.

nodes.misconception: Nazi concentration camps and extermination camps were the same thing.
nodes.response: Concentration camps were used for imprisonment, forced labour and punishment, not initially for mass murder. Extermination camps, built later, were designed specifically for killing on an industrial scale.

nodes.misconception: A common misconception is that a small increase in greenhouse gases and a small rise in Earth's temperature will not have much impact on organisms on Earth beyond polar ice melting.
nodes.response: The lesson outlines how human activities increase the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere and how this links to climate change. The lesson also outlines how climate change impacts life on Earth.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think lines with gradients 2 and -2 are parallel.
nodes.response: Lines have to have the exact same gradient to be parallel. A line with a negative gradient will intersect a line with a positive gradient .

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that Mandela ended apartheid on his own.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that he worked with many others to change the laws.

nodes.misconception: Learners may think that the inner loop only runs once per program, rather than repeating fully each time the outer loop runs.
nodes.response: The inner loop runs completely every time the outer loop runs once. This means the code inside the inner loop is repeated multiple times depending on how many times the outer loop is executed.

nodes.misconception: A nested selection statement can only have one nested selection block.
nodes.response: Selection statements can can continue to be nested in further selection blocks to provide more complex conditions for which specific code will be executed.

nodes.misconception: All devices on a network use the same IP address, so there’s no need for private or public IPs or DNS.
nodes.response: Each device needs a unique private IP address on a local network. To access the internet, the router uses a public IP address. DNS translates website names into IP addresses so devices know where to send data.

nodes.misconception: All networks must have a server because a server is always needed to share files or printers between devices.
nodes.response: Not all networks need a server. In a peer-to-peer model, each computer can act as both client and server, sharing files directly. This setup is simpler but may lack central control and security.

nodes.misconception: All devices on a network share the same MAC address because they’re connected to the same router.
nodes.response: Each network device has its own unique MAC address assigned to its network interface card (NIC).

nodes.misconception: The internet is built directly on the OSI 7-layer model, and its layers are actual physical hardware components.
nodes.response: The OSI model is a conceptual framework, not the internet's direct architecture. It helps to understand network functions.

nodes.misconception: The only factor that affects network performance is how fast your internet connection is.
nodes.response: Connection speed does affect performance, but it is also influenced by factors like bandwidth, latency, number of users, packet loss, hardware quality and interference on wireless networks.

nodes.misconception: Network security just stops viruses, so it’s only important for large organisations, not for individuals or small businesses.
nodes.response: Network security protects all users, not just large organisations. It prevents data theft, fraud, and service disruption. Individuals need protection from threats like phishing or ransomware.

nodes.misconception: All network topologies work the same way and have the same benefits.
nodes.response: Different topologies connect devices in different ways. For example, star networks use a central hub, while mesh networks connect devices directly. Each has unique strengths and weaknesses depending on the situation.

nodes.misconception: The imperfect tense is never used in spoken German.
nodes.response: The most common irregular verbs 'haben' and 'sein' are very common in speaking, along with 'es gab'. Other verbs in the imperfect mainly appear in written texts.

nodes.misconception: There is usually a lot of confusion over the synapse and how the signal moves from electrical, to chemical, to electrical again. There are many new key words involved, which makes it even harder.
nodes.response: The synapse has been broken down into several stages with clear diagrams and carefully used key words. There are plenty of opportunities to practise using the terminology and explaining the process, including applying it to a real-world scenario.

nodes.misconception: Germ Theory's accuracy meant that it was immediately accepted in Britain.
nodes.response: Many doctors still defended spontaneous generation and it took the additional proof provided by Robert Koch's work to convince many that microbes caused disease.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will look for any word with ‘a’ in it e.g. shared.   ‘A’ can be pronounced in different ways.
nodes.response: Remind pupils to stretch each word when reading to help hear the 'ay' sound e.g. s-t-a-b-le vs sh-are-d

nodes.misconception: All followers of the same religion practise their religion in the same way.
nodes.response: There are often large differences between followers of the same religion: people include elements of their own culture in their worship.

nodes.misconception: Translate reflexive verbs literally into English with the reflexive pronoun.
nodes.response: Some verbs use reflexive pronouns in French, but we don’t always translate the reflexive pronoun in English e.g. 'Je me sens' meaning 'I feel'.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will look for any word with ‘e’ in it and associate it with the long vowel 'ee'.
nodes.response: Teach that ‘e’ can be pronounced in different ways. Emphasise that in most words, the 'e' is making an 'e' phoneme.

nodes.misconception: The digraph 'or' and trigraph 'ear' also make different long vowel sounds.
nodes.response: Remind children that the same grapheme (digraph and trigraph) can represent different sounds.  Say the words out loud to check.

nodes.misconception: Like in English, most consonants are pronounced at the ends of words.
nodes.response: Many words have SFCs (silent final consonants) in which the last letter is not pronounced in French.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will look for any word with ‘i’ in it e.g. carried. ‘I’ can be pronounced in different ways.
nodes.response: Always tell children to read the word with the most common phoneme for the grapheme and check if it makes sense.

nodes.misconception: It is possible to view the British Empire as either a force for good or bad.
nodes.response: The enormity of the British Empire and number of individuals involved means that to attach a simple label to the British Empire is an impossible task.

nodes.misconception: Pupils will look for any word with ‘o’ in it and associate it with the long vowel 'oa'.
nodes.response: Teach that ‘o’ can be pronounced in different ways. Emphasise that in most words, the 'o' is making an 'o' phoneme.

nodes.misconception: The 'ou' and 'ui' spelling can be pronounced in different ways e.g. suit vs build or soup vs shout.
nodes.response: Be explicit with children about these different pronunciations and give them the opportunity to read words out loud to check.

nodes.misconception: Children can mix up the meaning of 'bought' and 'brought'.
nodes.response: Say the words in sentences several times to establish the meaning, and link to the present tense 'buy' and bring'.

nodes.misconception: Use one preposition for 'in' like in English.
nodes.response: There are a number of prepositions for 'in', depending on the number and gender of the noun. Use 'en' for feminine countries, à for cities, au with masculine nouns, à la with feminine nouns and aux with plural nouns and countries.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may have previously only seen a relative clause interrupting a main clause.
nodes.response: A relative clause can be placed after any noun it refers to, including at the end of a sentence.

nodes.misconception: The letter 'e' is always pronounced the same in French.
nodes.response: The letter 'e' is often pronounced as the 'e' in 'je' is but can be pronounced like [è/ê]. Pronounce 'e' like [è/ê] before double consonants and the letters c/l if they are in the last syllable.

nodes.misconception: Always use the verb 'avoir' to help you form the perfect tense.
nodes.response: Remember - for movement verbs and 'rester' use 'être', instead of 'avoir', to help you form the perfect tense.

nodes.misconception: 'Zu', meaning 'to', is always needed as part of two-verb infinitive structures, e.g., 'Ich hoffe, mehr in die Schule zu lernen.'.
nodes.response: 'Werden' and modal verbs do not need 'zu' before the second verb: 'Ich werde mehr in der Schule lernen'. Other verbs that do not require 'zu' include 'helfen', 'lassen' and 'mögen'.

nodes.misconception: When using two-verb constructions, the second verb is always in the infinitive and comes at the end of the clause.
nodes.response: When a two-verb construction follows a subordinating conjunction like ‘weil’, the short form of the verb moves to the end, after the infinitive (WO3), e.g., ‘Ich hoffe, dieses Jahr zu feiern, weil es Spaß machen wird.’.

nodes.misconception: Like in English, there is just one way of saying 'you' in French.
nodes.response: In French there are in fact two ways of saying you. Use 'tu' when talking to one young person or to an adult you know well. Use 'vous' when talking to more than one person or to one adult you do not know well.

nodes.misconception: To say what 'we do' instead of what 'I do' in Spanish, you just change the pronoun from 'I' to 'we' and keep the verb the same.
nodes.response: In Spanish it's the verb ending and not the pronoun that changes the subject of the verb, so you need to pay close attention to the verb form to know who is doing the action of the verb, e.g. 'I sell' - 'vendo', 'we sell' - 'vendemos'.

nodes.misconception: 'Que' means 'what' in Spanish.
nodes.response: 'Qué' with an accent on the 'e' is the question word 'what'. 'Que' without an accent is a conjunction meaning 'that' - 'Creo que hay una solución'.

nodes.misconception: Cognate recognition is the only strategy I need to understand texts in German.
nodes.response: Cognates are helpful, but not always enough.  You will understand much more if you know some common word and spelling patterns in German, and if you use your vocabulary and grammar knowledge creatively to work out the meanings of unfamiliar words.

nodes.misconception: When telling a story about a past event, I have to keep the full account in the same past tense.
nodes.response: Different past tenses describe different elements of a story. The imperfect continuous describes what was happening ('Estaba corriendo ...') then the preterite tense describes an interruption to that activity ('... cuando llegó una vaca'.).

nodes.misconception: In the imperfect continuous I can tell who the subject of the verb is by looking at the form of 'estar' being used.
nodes.response: The 'I' and 'he, she, it' forms of the imperfect tense of 'estar' are the same: 'estaba'. Therefore you have to use the context to work out who the subject of the verb is when this form is being used.

nodes.misconception: Pupils believe driving forces are needed to keep objects moving at constant speed.
nodes.response: Demonstrate that friction (and drag) bring objects to a stop, showing that different surfaces produce the forces that slow objects.

nodes.misconception: When applying the equation F = m × a, pupils may take F to be any one of the forces acting on the object, rather than specifically the resultant force.
nodes.response: Provide some more complex examples, in which forces act in opposite directions, so pupils are required to work out the resultant force in preparation for completing calculations.

nodes.misconception: When applying the equation F = m × a, pupils may take F to be any one of the forces acting on the object, rather than specifically the resultant force.
nodes.response: Provide some more complex examples, in which forces act in opposite directions, so pupils are required to work out the resultant force in preparation for completing calculations.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may regard force as a property of an object, expressing ideas such as ‘the object has a force’ and ‘the object runs out of force’.
nodes.response: Describe forces as interactions between two objects, using the phrasing ‘the force of object A on object B’.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may regard force as a property of an object, expressing ideas such as ‘the object has a force’ and ‘the object runs out of force’.
nodes.response: Describe forces as interactions between two objects, using the phrasing ‘the force of object A on object B’.

nodes.misconception: Nibbana (Nirvana) is a Buddhist view of heaven.
nodes.response: Nibbana is the cessation of suffering, craving and ignorance. It is the end of the cycle of rebirth and the realisation of true peace and freedom.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that most early astronomy was conducted using telescopes.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that astronomers didn’t have telescopes, so they used their eyes and mathematical calculations to help them.

nodes.misconception: Globalisation is the world becoming more developed.
nodes.response: Globalisation is the world becoming more interconnected.

nodes.misconception: Old stories have no relevance.
nodes.response: There are meanings in stories even when they are old and confusing.

nodes.misconception: Children may think that any sound is classified as noise, or that only very loud sounds are considered to be noise pollution.
nodes.response: Explain that unpleasant or unwanted sounds are classified as noise. Noise pollution does not have to be loud, it can be an intermittent or continuous quieter noise that becomes a problem.

nodes.misconception: The outcomes of a trial are always equally likely to occur (e.g. each of the two players in a tennis match are equally likely to win).
nodes.response: There are factors that may affect how likely one outcome is compared to another (e.g. the skill or experience of one tennis player compared to the other).

nodes.misconception: Once planned, I just need to take part in the training without writing anything down.
nodes.response: It is useful to keep up to date training logs for each session to help monitor progress (these are not included in the word count) as well as doing mid PEP fitness testing to check progress and adapt the planned training programme where needed.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think a horizontal line on a speed-time means the object is stationary.
nodes.response: The $$y$$ axis is plotting speed so a horizontal line means the speed has not changed in that time. But this can be at any speed. Pupils need to double check axes to know what sort of graph they are using.

nodes.misconception: Only religious people believe in life after death.
nodes.response: People who aren't religious often believe in some sort of life after death; this can range from believing in a soul which lives on to believing that our legacy lives on.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may mix-up the x and y coordinates.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that the x value is read from the x-axis and is read first. The y value is read from the y-axis and is read second.

nodes.misconception: All blood cells protect us against pathogens.
nodes.response: White blood cells are part of the immune system that protects us against pathogens. Red blood cells transport oxygen to cells. Platelets are not cells, but they do help to protect against pathogens by helping to seal wounds.

nodes.misconception: Content alone is enough for an effective speech.
nodes.response: Consider the most engaging speakers and how they use tone, gestures and eye contact. Giving a speech is so much more than just the words on a page.

nodes.misconception: Content alone is enough for an effective speech.
nodes.response: Consider the most engaging speakers and how they use tone, gestures and eye contact. Giving a speech is so much more than just the words on a page.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that power associated with land ownership was a Norman import to England.
nodes.response: Remind pupils that Anglo-Saxon England was a society largely based on land ownership and the power that this brought.

nodes.misconception: The written word is the only useful source for the study of the past.
nodes.response: Although written sources are useful, material remains can reveal much about past societies - it depends on the questions historians ask of the source.

nodes.misconception: The Anglo-Saxon Church was old-fashioned and corrupt.
nodes.response: The Normans were keen to present the Anglo-Saxon Church that way, but Edward the Confessor had kept up with reforms from the rest of Europe.

nodes.misconception: Monks were all poor.
nodes.response: Although individual monks gave up all their possessions, Norman monasteries were often extremely wealthy because they held very large amount of land granted to them by the king or Norman barons and knights.

nodes.misconception: Students might think that 'the Church' is a physical building in which people pray.
nodes.response: Explain that 'the Church' refers to the wider organisation of the Christian faith, including all buildings and people which belong to it.

nodes.misconception: The Anglo-Saxon Church was old-fashioned and corrupt.
nodes.response: The Normans were keen to present the Anglo-Saxon Church that way, but Edward the Confessor had kept up with reforms from the rest of Europe.

nodes.misconception: Students commonly do not provide enough detail from their historic environment in their answers.
nodes.response: Try to back up your analysis of the question with specific facts and details from your historic environment.

nodes.misconception: Castles built by the Normans were designed to intimidate the local Anglo-Saxons and provided no benefit for them.
nodes.response: One of the primary functions of castles was to intimidate the local population, but castles also frequently drew people to them and created an urban centre, which boosted the local economy.

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like listening out for synonyms and distractors to do well in my listening exam.
nodes.response: Strategies like listening out for synonyms and distractors are useful for listening exams, but the most important thing is to have a broad vocabulary.

nodes.misconception: I can rely on strategies like listening out for synonyms and distractors to do well in my listening exam.
nodes.response: Strategies like listening out for synonyms and distractors are useful for listening exams, but the most important thing is to have a broad vocabulary.

nodes.misconception: Verbs must always have different subjects and objects.
nodes.response: Verbs do not always have different subjects and objects. For example, reflexive verbs have the same subject and object.

nodes.misconception: When translating from Spanish to English, I should translate each word in the order it appears in the Spanish sentence.
nodes.response: When translating from Spanish to English, make sure your translations sound natural in English. This may mean you need to change the word order from the original Spanish sentence.

nodes.misconception: When translating from Spanish to English, I should translate each word in the order it appears in the Spanish sentence.
nodes.response: When translating from Spanish to English, make sure your translations sound natural in English. This may mean you need to change the word order from the original Spanish sentence.

nodes.misconception: I should translate each English word individually when translating into Spanish.
nodes.response: It is important to read the whole sentence first and translate chunks of language rather than each individual word.

nodes.misconception: I should translate each English word individually when translating into Spanish.
nodes.response: It is important to read the whole sentence first and translate chunks of language rather than each individual word.

nodes.misconception: I should give long, developed answers to role-play prompts.
nodes.response: It is not necessary to give long, developed answers to role-play prompts. It is best to respond using a short phrase or sentence.

nodes.misconception: Ta-di and Ta-mi are the same because they both have two notes in one beat.
nodes.response: With the Ta-di rhythm both notes divide the beat equally in half. With Ta-mi, the notes are not distributed equally - the first is longer (¾ of a beat) and the second is shorter (¼ of a beat).

nodes.misconception: The word low is sometimes associated with quiet.
nodes.response: The word low refers to pitch.

nodes.misconception: High and low refers to volume (loud and quiet).
nodes.response: High and low refers to pitch.

nodes.misconception: The note la is placed anywhere above the high line on the stave.
nodes.response: The note la sits on top of and touches the high line of the stave.

nodes.misconception: When using 'venir de' (to have just), the next word needs to be a past participle, like in English.
nodes.response: In French, 'venir de' is like every other French verb followed by 'de'. It is always followed by a second verb in the infinitive.

nodes.misconception: If a source has a limitation then it is not reliable or useful for a historical study.
nodes.response: All sources have limitations as well as strengths, which historians take account of, and does not mean that the source should not be used by a historian.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that proper nouns only have a capital letter at the start of a sentence.
nodes.response: Pupils will be exposed to a range of sentences in which proper nouns feature at the beginning, middle and end.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may think that any noun ending is 's' is a plural noun.
nodes.response: Pupils are exposed to singular nouns that end in the letter 's'.

nodes.misconception: Ammonia and ammonium are the same thing.
nodes.response: Carefully compare the different chemical formulae, structures, and distinct uses in fertilisers vs. industrial applications. Use visual aids to reinforce these differences.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not have a clear understanding of the forces acting between neutrons and protons in an atomic nucleus.
nodes.response: In simple terms, explain the reasons why some nuclei are unstable in terms of electrostatic repulsion, and include ideas about the strong nuclear force attracting protons and neutrons to each other.

nodes.misconception: Pupils may not have a clear understanding of the forces acting between neutrons and protons in an atomic nucleus.
nodes.response: In simple terms, explain the reasons why some nuclei are unstable in terms of electrostatic repulsion, and include ideas about the strong nuclear force attracting protons and neutrons to each other.

nodes.misconception: Radioactive isotopes disappear when they decay, so that in one half-life half the mass is lost.
